subject: science
stem: Meena is preparing a school science chart at her home in Jaipur. She writes: 'In a plant cell, one structure alone gives the cell its firmness and rigidity.' Her younger brother says the cell membrane does this job. Which structure should Meena name on her chart?

options.A: cell membrane
options.B: cell wall
options.C: nucleus
options.D: cytoplasm

subject: science
stem: Meera's teacher shows the class slides of different human cells under a microscope. One cell is very long and thin, with thread-like branches. Which statement best explains how this shape helps the cell perform its specific function?

options.A: The long, branched shape helps the nerve cell carry messages quickly over long distances in the body.
options.B: The long, branched shape helps the cheek cell form a flat protective lining inside the mouth.
options.C: The long, branched shape helps the muscle cell contract and relax to move body parts.
options.D: The long, branched shape helps the red blood cell carry more oxygen through its round disc shape.

subject: science
stem: In her school laboratory, Meena observes two cells under a microscope during a biology practical in Pune. Cell P is thin and flat, forming a protective lining on the inside of the cheek. Cell Q is very long with thread-like branches and carries messages between the brain and the rest of the body. Which statement best explains how the shape and structure of each cell suit its function?

options.A: Cell P is thin and flat, which helps it form a protective layer, while Cell Q is long and branched, which helps it carry messages quickly over long distances.
options.B: Cell P is long and branched so it can carry messages, while Cell Q is thin and flat so it can form a protective lining.
options.C: Both cells have the same shape because they come from the same person's body, and their shape does not affect their function.
options.D: Cell Q is long because carrying messages stretches it out over time, while Cell P is flat because it has no specific function.

subject: science
stem: Meena's science teacher in her school in Pune asks the class to place the stomach of a human being at the correct level of organisation. In the sequence cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism, where does the stomach belong?

options.A: cell
options.B: tissue
options.C: organ
options.D: organ system

subject: science
stem: In her Science class, Meera learns that her body is organised in levels: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism. Her heart is made of muscle tissue and pumps blood around her body. In this sequence of levels, the heart is best described as an:

options.A: organ system
options.B: tissue
options.C: organ
options.D: organism

subject: science
stem:
Ravi looked at a drop of pond water under a microscope in his school laboratory in Patna. He saw a tiny Amoeba moving about, feeding and reproducing, all on its own.
Ravi said, "It has only one cell, so it cannot be a complete living organism."
Which statement about the Amoeba is correct?

options.A: It is a complete living organism because one cell carries out all the functions needed for survival.
options.B: It is not a living organism because all living organisms are made of many cells.
options.C: It is alive only when it joins with other Amoeba cells to form a group.
options.D: It is a complete organism only because it lives in pond water.

subject: science
stem: During a science class in Meerut, Riya looks at a drop of pond water under the microscope and sees a single-celled Amoeba moving and feeding on its own. Her classmate Arjun says, “It has only one cell, so it cannot be a complete living organism.” Which statement is correct?

options.A: Arjun is correct, because every living organism must be made of many cells.
options.B: Riya is correct to disagree, because the single cell of an Amoeba carries out all life processes, so it is a complete organism.
options.C: Arjun is correct, because unicellular organisms can feed but cannot reproduce on their own.
options.D: Neither is correct, because an Amoeba becomes a complete organism only after joining with other cells.

subject: science
stem: Meera collects a drop of pond water and a pinch of moist soil mixed in water for her class project. Under a microscope she sees many tiny moving beings, but she can see nothing in these samples with her unaided eye. What should she conclude about these tiny moving beings?

options.A: They are microorganisms, because they are living beings too small to be seen with the unaided eye.
options.B: They are not microorganisms, because the pond water and soil look like plain dirt to the unaided eye.
options.C: They are not microorganisms, because microorganisms are found only in water and never in moist soil.
options.D: They are not microorganisms, because anything that moves under a microscope must be a non-living particle.

subject: science
stem: Meena collects a few drops of water from a pond near her school in Jaipur. To her unaided eye, the water looks clear with nothing living in it. Under a foldscope, she sees many tiny moving specks that she could not see before. What should Meena conclude about these tiny moving specks?

options.A: They are not living beings, because clear pond water cannot contain any organisms.
options.B: They are small dust particles, because anything invisible to the unaided eye must be nonliving.
options.C: They are microorganisms, because they are tiny living beings that can only be seen with magnification.
options.D: They are large insects, because only insects can live in pond water.

subject: science
stem: Meera looks at a drop of pond water under her school microscope in Surat and sees a tiny living thing that changes shape as it moves by pushing out part of its body. Which group does this organism belong to?

options.A: virus
options.B: bacterium
options.C: protozoan
options.D: fungus

subject: science
stem: During a school science exhibition in Jaipur, Meena displays four samples she collected at home: an Amoeba seen in pond water, bread mould grown on a stale roti, a culture of bacteria from curd, and a virus sample studied from a chart. Her teacher asks her to label each sample correctly. Which row of her chart is correct?

options.A: Amoeba – protozoan; bread mould – fungus; bacteria – bacterium; virus – multiplies only inside living cells
options.B: Amoeba – bacterium; bread mould – protozoan; bacteria – fungus; virus – an alga
options.C: Amoeba – protozoan; bread mould – bacterium; bacteria – fungus; virus – multiplies outside living cells
options.D: All four samples are bacteria because they are all microscopic

subject: science
stem:
Meera keeps four bowls of cooked dal on the kitchen table in her home in Pune for two days. The table shows the condition of each bowl.
In which bowl are microorganisms most likely to grow and spoil the dal?

options.A: dal mixed with a large amount of salt
options.B: plain dal left uncovered in warm air
options.C: dal mixed with a large amount of sugar
options.D: dal kept covered in the refrigerator

subject: science
stem: Meena left a bowl of cooked dal uncovered on the kitchen counter, and by the next morning it had turned sour. Beside it, a jar of mango pickle made with plenty of salt and oil stayed fresh for many months. Which statement best explains why the dal rotted but the pickle did not get infected in the same way?

options.A: The dal rotted because it was naturally weak, while the pickle stayed safe simply because it is a pickle.
options.B: Microorganisms from the air and surroundings settled on the exposed dal and made it rot, while the high salt in the pickle acted as a preservative that prevented microbial infection.
options.C: The dal rotted first and the rotting itself produced the microorganisms that soured it.
options.D: Only a large amount of salt or sugar can stop microorganisms, so the small amount of salt in the pickle played no role in keeping it fresh.

subject: science
stem: Meera adds vegetable peels and cow dung to a closed pit in her garden in Nagpur. After a few weeks, the waste turns into dark, nutrient-rich manure. Which organisms are mainly responsible for this change?

options.A: Earthworms that eat the waste and convert it into manure on their own
options.B: Bacteria and fungi that decompose the waste into simpler substances
options.C: Algae growing on the surface that release nutrients from sunlight
options.D: Viruses present in the soil that break down the waste

subject: science
stem: Meera's class sets up a pit behind the school garden where vegetable peels, fallen leaves and cow dung are buried for several weeks. Later, the material has turned into dark, crumbly manure. What best explains how this change happened?

options.A: Soil fungi and bacteria slowly broke down the plant and animal waste into simpler, nutrient-rich manure.
options.B: The peels and dung dried out in the pit and turned into manure on their own.
options.C: The buried waste attracted microorganisms, which then fed on the ready-made manure.
options.D: Microorganisms need plenty of open air and sunlight to change the waste into manure.

subject: science
stem:
Meena prepares two balls of dough in her kitchen in Jaipur. She mixes yeast, sugar and warm water into the first ball, but leaves yeast out of the second ball. After one hour, only the first ball of dough has risen.

Why does the dough with yeast rise while the dough without yeast does not rise in the same way?

options.A: The yeast is broken down by the flour and turns into gas.
options.B: The yeast respires, releasing carbon dioxide gas that makes the dough expand.
options.C: The warm water alone produces gas in any dough left for one hour.
options.D: The yeast absorbs air from the kitchen and stores it in the dough.

subject: science
stem:
Meena's mother mixes wheat flour with yeast, sugar and warm water to make dough. After one hour the dough rises and becomes larger in size. She makes a second dough in the same way but without yeast, and it does not rise in the same way.
Why does the dough with yeast rise?

options.A: Yeast is a microorganism that grows in the warm dough and makes the dough rise after some time.
options.B: Warm water and flour rise on their own, so the yeast is not needed at all.
options.C: Yeast is only a flavouring powder and the sugar alone makes the dough rise.
options.D: The dough rises first, which then gives the yeast enough room to grow in it.

subject: science
stem: Meera mixes a small spoonful of curd into a bowl of lukewarm milk and another spoonful into a bowl of cold milk, and leaves both for a few hours. Only the lukewarm milk sets into curd. What best explains this difference?

options.A: Cold milk contains more water than lukewarm milk, so it cannot set.
options.B: The microorganisms in the curd starter grow and multiply faster at warm temperatures, turning the milk into curd.
options.C: Both bowls form curd equally fast, so the difference is only in how sour they taste.
options.D: Warmth kills the microorganisms in the starter, so lukewarm milk sets while cold milk stays liquid.

subject: science
stem: Priya's mother mixes a spoonful of curd into two bowls of milk. Bowl 1 has warm milk; bowl 2 has milk straight from the refrigerator. After five hours, only bowl 1 has set into firm curd. What is the best reason for this difference?

options.A: The bacteria in the starter grow and multiply faster at warm temperatures, so they turn the milk into curd quickly.
options.B: Cold milk contains fewer nutrients, so the bacteria in the starter cannot use it.
options.C: Warmth kills all the harmful microorganisms in the milk, allowing curd to form.
options.D: The refrigerator adds extra water to the milk, which stops curd from setting.

subject: science
stem:
Meena's teacher asks the class why conserving microalgae in ponds and lakes matters.
Which reason is correct?

options.A: Microalgae use sunlight to make their own food and help keep the oxygen balance of the environment.
options.B: Microalgae supply nitrogen to the air instead of oxygen when they make food using sunlight.
options.C: Microalgae can keep making their own food by the same process even in permanent darkness.
options.D: Conserving microalgae increases pollution because abundant microalgae cause it.

subject: science
stem: Meera's class in Nagpur visits a pond where tiny plant-like organisms called microalgae grow. Her teacher explains that these microalgae use sunlight to make their own food. Why does Meera's teacher say that conserving microalgae matters?

options.A: Microalgae add nitrogen to the air when they make food using sunlight.
options.B: Microalgae help maintain oxygen balance and support food security and livelihoods.
options.C: Microalgae can keep making their own food using sunlight even in permanent darkness.
options.D: Conserving microalgae increases pollution because abundant microalgae cause it.

subject: science
stem:
Which of the following statements about health is correct ( )
A. Ravi is healthy because no disease has been found in his body
B. Meena is free from illness but feels lonely and cannot sleep well, so she is fully healthy
C. A person is healthy only when physical, mental, and social well-being are all present, not merely when disease is absent
D. Arjun has strong muscles and plays cricket daily, so he must be healthy even if he is often worried and has no friends

options.A: Ravi is healthy because no disease has been found in his body
options.B: Meena is free from illness but feels lonely and cannot sleep well, so she is fully healthy
options.C: A person is healthy only when physical, mental, and social well-being are all present, not merely when disease is absent
options.D: Arjun has strong muscles and plays cricket daily, so he must be healthy even if he is often worried and has no friends

subject: science
stem:
Meena's school in Nagpur held a health check-up week. The teacher asked the class to decide who among the following students can be called truly healthy. Whose situation shows complete health ( )
A. Arjun has no disease, but he feels lonely, sleeps poorly, and avoids his classmates
B. Kavya is free from illness, eats balanced food, stays cheerful, and shares a good bond with her friends and family
C. Ravi has strong muscles and wins races, so he must be healthy even though he often quarrels with everyone
D. Sana has no fever or cough this month, so nothing else needs to be checked

options.A: Arjun has no disease, but he feels lonely, sleeps poorly, and avoids his classmates
options.B: Kavya is free from illness, eats balanced food, stays cheerful, and shares a good bond with her friends and family
options.C: Ravi has strong muscles and wins races, so he must be healthy even though he often quarrels with everyone
options.D: Sana has no fever or cough this month, so nothing else needs to be checked

subject: science
stem:
Meera's class discussed daily habits and surroundings that support a healthy body and a healthy mind. Which of the following statements is incorrect ( )
A. Eating nutritious food and keeping the home and school surroundings clean support good health
B. Regular exercise and enough sleep every night help Meera stay healthy
C. Only physical fitness matters for health, so Meera's friendship with Aisha and a positive attitude do not count
D. Good personal hygiene, like washing hands before meals, protects the body from illness

options.A: Eating nutritious food and keeping the home and school surroundings clean support good health
options.B: Regular exercise and enough sleep every night help Meera stay healthy
options.C: Only physical fitness matters for health, so Meera's friendship with Aisha and a positive attitude do not count
options.D: Good personal hygiene, like washing hands before meals, protects the body from illness

subject: science
stem:
Meena lives in a small town in Rajasthan. She wants to keep her body and mind healthy.
Which of her daily habits best supports good health?

options.A: staying awake late at night watching videos on her phone
options.B: eating a balanced meal, sleeping on time, and playing outside with friends
options.C: eating only the sweets she likes most because they taste good
options.D: keeping her classroom clean but ignoring the broken furniture and unsafe corners

subject: science
stem: Meera's teacher says that a person is unwell when something in the body or mind is not working normally. Which student's situation does NOT show that the student is unwell?

options.A: Arjun has a high fever and body ache since morning
options.B: Sana feels dizzy and cannot stand steadily during assembly
options.C: Rohan feels tired after running in a school race but recovers after a short rest
options.D: Priya has been unable to concentrate or sleep properly for many days

subject: science
stem:
During the morning assembly at a school in Pune, Ravi feels dizzy and has a headache, although he was fine the day before. His teacher says he seems unwell.

Why is Ravi considered unwell?

options.A: His signs show that his body is not working as it normally should.
options.B: He was completely healthy the previous day.
options.C: His discomfort is not severe, so he can keep attending classes.
options.D: Only a serious disease can make a person unwell.

subject: science
stem: In Meena's class in Delhi, three students caught chickenpox within two weeks. The school nurse explains that chickenpox is caused by a virus and passes from one person to another through the air and by touch. How should this disease be classified?

options.A: communicable disease
options.B: non-communicable disease
options.C: chronic disease
options.D: lifestyle disease

subject: science
stem: Meena's younger brother Arjun caught chickenpox. It is caused by a virus, and within a few days two other children in his class in Jaipur also fell ill after playing with him. How should this disease be classified?

options.A: Non-communicable, because it is caused by a virus inside the body
options.B: Communicable, because it is caused by a pathogen and spreads from person to person
options.C: Chronic, because it can last for more than a week
options.D: Non-communicable, because it cannot spread through air or water

subject: science
stem: Meera's classmate Rohan has influenza, which spreads through cough droplets in the air. During the school day, which step will best protect Meera from catching Rohan's influenza?

options.A: washing her hands once after the morning assembly
options.B: drinking water from the tap because it looks clear
options.C: wearing a mask and sitting away from Rohan while he coughs
options.D: making sure she never touches Rohan's towel

subject: science
stem:
Meena's younger brother in their home in Nagpur has chickenpox, which spreads when the pathogen passes from an infected person to others through close contact and through contaminated articles like shared towels and bedding.
Which single step best prevents the disease from spreading to the rest of the family?

options.A: Keep the brother's towels, bedsheets and utensils separate and wash hands after touching them
options.B: Make sure everyone in the house drinks boiled water at every meal
options.C: Spray the rooms every evening to kill mosquitoes
options.D: Give the whole family vitamin tablets so they do not fall ill

subject: science
stem: Meena's father in Pune has been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. The doctor explains how the family should manage his condition. Which statement gives the correct approach to controlling this non-communicable disease?

options.A: One complete course of diabetes medicine will cure him permanently, so no further care is needed.
options.B: Reducing his physical activity will lower his risk of heart disease.
options.C: He needs continuous care, regular checkups, a balanced diet, and daily exercise to manage the disease.
options.D: Since he looks healthy, he does not need regular checkups or any change in lifestyle.

subject: science
stem: Rohan's grandfather in Lucknow has been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. His doctor explains that this non-communicable disease cannot be cured in a few days, but it can be controlled. Which approach will best control his condition?

options.A: Taking one full course of medicine so that no further care is needed
options.B: Reducing physical activity so that the risk of heart disease also falls
options.C: Keeping him away from other family members for a few days
options.D: Managing the condition with regular medicine, a balanced diet, exercise and continuous checkups

subject: science
stem: In a government school in Pune, a measles vaccination camp is held before the monsoon. Meera's grandmother asks why healthy children are being vaccinated. Which statement best explains how vaccination reduces serious infections and their spread?

options.A: Vaccines are medicines taken after someone falls sick, so they cure measles and stop it spreading.
options.B: Vaccines prepare the immune system before exposure, so vaccinated children are less likely to become seriously ill and less likely to pass the infection to others.
options.C: The first exposure to measles produces the stronger immune response, so vaccination is only useful after a child has already had measles once.
options.D: Children in the same class share the same immunity, so vaccinating a few children protects the whole class equally.

subject: science
stem:
Meena's school in Nagpur runs a measles vaccination camp for all children in Class 8. The health worker explains that vaccinated children are very unlikely to become seriously ill with measles.

How does vaccination reduce serious measles infections and their spread in the school?

options.A: It cures measles in children who are already sick, so they stop spreading it.
options.B: It prepares the immune system to fight the measles virus before exposure, so fewer children fall ill and pass it on.
options.C: It kills all the measles viruses present in the classroom air.
options.D: It replaces the need for the immune system to respond to the virus.

subject: science
stem: Meena has a sore throat and fever. Her mother wants to give her leftover antibiotic tablets from an earlier illness. The doctor advises against this. Why should antibiotics be taken only when a doctor prescribes them for a bacterial infection?

options.A: Antibiotics work against every infection, so taking them early always cures the illness faster.
options.B: Antibiotics kill bacteria, and careless use can let resistant bacteria develop, making future infections harder to treat.
options.C: Antibiotics first act on the throat and then on the stomach, so they must be taken with food.
options.D: Antibiotics become stronger each time they are used, so frequent use keeps them powerful.

subject: science
stem: Meena, a student in Jaipur, has a sore throat and mild fever. Her doctor checks her and says it is a viral cold, so no antibiotic is needed. Later, her uncle takes leftover antibiotic tablets whenever he feels slightly unwell. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Antibiotics are suitable for every infection, so Meena should take them for her cold.
options.B: Antibiotics kill bacteria, but careless use lets resistant bacteria develop, so the same antibiotic becomes less effective.
options.C: Careless antibiotic use makes bacteria easier to kill, so the same antibiotic becomes more effective.
options.D: A fever alone means an antibiotic is needed, so Meena must start antibiotics immediately.

subject: science
stem:
Meera connects a straight copper wire to a cell in her classroom and holds a small compass close to the wire. She presses the switch and current flows through the wire.
What happens to the compass needle, and why?

options.A: The needle deflects because the current in the wire produces a magnetic field around the wire
options.B: The needle deflects only after the wire becomes hot
options.C: The needle does not deflect because copper is not a magnetic material
options.D: The needle deflects because the cell attracts the needle directly

subject: science
stem:
Meena connects a copper wire to a cell in her classroom in Jaipur. She holds a magnetic compass close to the wire and then presses the switch so that current flows through the wire.
What should happen to the compass needle, and why?

options.A: The needle deflects, because the current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field around it.
options.B: The needle does not move, because a compass needle moves only near a permanent magnet.
options.C: The needle deflects only after the wire becomes hot from the current.
options.D: The needle does not move, because copper is not a magnetic material.

subject: science
stem: Kavya places a compass next to a copper coil that can be switched into a closed loop with a cell. Which statements should be true?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1 only

statements.text: When the switch is ON and the loop is complete, the compass needle should deflect.
When the switch is ON but a wire is disconnected, the needle should still deflect because the cell is present.
A resting compass, by itself, drives a steady current through the nearby coil.

subject: science
stem:
Meena wraps an insulated copper wire around an iron nail and connects the ends to a cell to make an electromagnet for a school project. She uses it to pick up steel paper clips.
Which statement about her electromagnet is correct?

options.A: The nail stays magnetised and keeps holding the clips even after the current is switched off.
options.B: The iron nail inside the coil makes the electromagnet weaker.
options.C: Without the iron nail, the current-carrying coil cannot behave like a magnet at all.
options.D: The current-carrying coil behaves like a magnet, and the iron nail inside the coil makes the electromagnet stronger.

subject: science
stem:
For a school science exhibition, Meera wraps 40 turns of insulated copper wire around an iron nail and connects the ends to a dry cell. When the current flows, the nail picks up several steel paper clips. When she disconnects the cell, the clips fall off.
What do these observations show?

options.A: The coil acts as a temporary magnet only while current flows, and the iron nail makes the electromagnet stronger.
options.B: The coil acts as a permanent magnet, and the iron nail makes the electromagnet weaker.
options.C: The coil cannot act as a magnet unless the iron nail inside it heats up first.
options.D: The iron nail becomes a permanent magnet and keeps attracting the clips even without current.

subject: science
stem: Meena winds a coil of insulated copper wire around an iron nail and connects it to a cell to make an electromagnet. She brings the north pole of a small magnetic compass near end X of the nail, and the compass needle is attracted towards X. What does this show about the two ends of the electromagnet?

options.A: End X is a South pole and end Y is a North pole.
options.B: End X is a North pole and end Y is a South pole.
options.C: Both ends X and Y are North poles.
options.D: Both ends X and Y are South poles.

subject: science
stem:
Meena makes an electromagnet by winding an insulated copper wire around an iron nail and connecting the wire to a cell. When she brings the north pole of a magnetic compass near end X of the nail, the compass needle's north pole is attracted towards end X.
What are the polarities of the two ends of the electromagnet?

options.A: end X is North and end Y is South
options.B: end X is South and end Y is North
options.C: both end X and end Y are North
options.D: both end X and end Y are South

subject: science
stem:
In a scrapyard near Pune, Sameer uses a lifting electromagnet attached to a crane to move iron sheets.

When the current in the electromagnet is switched ON, what happens to the iron sheet, and what happens to it when the current is switched OFF?

options.A: ON: the iron sheet is released. OFF: the iron sheet is lifted.
options.B: ON: the iron sheet is lifted. OFF: the iron sheet is released.
options.C: ON: the iron sheet is lifted. OFF: the iron sheet keeps being held.
options.D: ON: the iron sheet is released. OFF: the iron sheet stays released.

subject: science
stem: In a scrapyard near Surat, Ravi uses a lifting electromagnet to move iron sheets. He has lifted an iron sheet and wants to drop it onto a truck. What should he do to release the iron sheet?

options.A: Switch the current ON so the electromagnet holds the sheet more tightly
options.B: Switch the current OFF so the magnetic effect stops and the sheet is released
options.C: Increase the current so the sheet falls off on its own
options.D: Wait, because the electromagnet keeps holding the sheet even without current

subject: science
stem:
Priya connects a nichrome wire to a cell in her school laboratory. After a few minutes, she notices that the wire has become warm.

Which statement correctly explains why the wire becomes warm?

options.A: The wire becomes warm simply because the cell is connected; current plays no part in heating.
options.B: The wire becomes warm first, and its warmth then makes the electric current flow through it.
options.C: Only nichrome wires become warm when an electric current flows; copper wires never do.
options.D: The current flowing through the wire meets resistance, and this resistance produces heat in the wire.

subject: science
stem:
Priya switches on the electric room heater at her home in Jaipur. After a few minutes, the nichrome coil inside the heater becomes warm and glows.
Why does the nichrome coil become warm when the heater is switched on?

options.A: The coil becomes warm simply because the switch is connected to the mains supply.
options.B: Current flows through the coil, the resistance of nichrome opposes the current, and heat is produced.
options.C: The coil becomes warm first, and its warmth then makes the electric current flow.
options.D: Only nichrome wires become warm; the current passes through them without any resistance.

subject: science
stem:
Meena connects the same nichrome wire first to one cell and then to two cells, each time for exactly 5 minutes, and compares the heat produced. Her brother says the heating of wires is always a bad thing.
Which statement is correct?

options.A: Two cells produce more heat in the same time, but all electrical heating is harmful, including in an electric iron.
options.B: Two cells produce more heat in the same time than one cell, and this heating is useful in appliances like an iron but harmful when a plug overheats.
options.C: One cell produces more heat than two cells in the same wire over the same time, and this heating is useful in an electric iron.
options.D: The same wire produces the same heat with one cell or two cells in 5 minutes, so overheating at a plug cannot happen.

subject: science
stem: Priya connects the same nichrome wire first to one cell and then to two cells, keeping it connected for the same time in both cases. She also notices that the plug of her electric iron becomes warm after long use. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The wire becomes hotter with one cell than with two cells, and the warm plug of the iron shows useful heating.
options.B: The wire becomes hotter with two cells than with one cell, but the warm plug of the iron is harmful heating that may damage the plug.
options.C: Neither wire becomes hotter because the wire does not glow in either case.
options.D: The wire becomes hotter with two cells than with one cell, and all heating produced by electricity is useful.

subject: science
stem:
Meera does a science activity at home in Jaipur. She puts two strips of metal into a lemon and connects them with wires to a small lamp.
Which setup will work as a cell and make the lamp glow?

options.A: two copper strips pushed into the lemon and connected to the lamp
options.B: a copper strip and an iron strip pushed into the lemon and connected to the lamp
options.C: a copper strip and an iron strip placed in a glass of plain water and connected to the lamp
options.D: a copper strip and an iron strip held in the air above the lemon and connected to the lamp

subject: science
stem:
Priya wants to make a small cell at home to light an LED, like the lemon cell she saw in class. She tries four different setups.

Setup 1: a copper strip and an iron nail pushed into a lemon, joined by wires to the LED.
Setup 2: two copper strips pushed into a lemon, joined by wires to the LED.
Setup 3: a copper strip and an iron nail placed in a dry plastic box, joined by wires to the LED.
Setup 4: two iron nails pushed into a lemon, joined by wires to the LED.

In which setup will the LED glow?

options.A: Setup 2, because two copper strips in a lemon always produce electricity
options.B: Setup 1, because it has two electrodes of different metals and the lemon juice acts as an electrolyte
options.C: Setup 4, because iron is a better conductor than copper
options.D: Setup 3, because keeping the electrodes dry makes the cell safer and stronger

subject: science
stem: Meera buys a cell for her torch at a shop in Jaipur. In this cell, the electrolyte is in the form of a moist paste rather than a free liquid, so the cell can be carried and used easily in everyday devices. Which type of cell is this?

options.A: a Voltaic cell, because it always contains a liquid electrolyte
options.B: a dry cell, because its electrolyte is a paste and it is convenient for daily use
options.C: a solar cell, because it uses sunlight to produce current
options.D: a dynamo, because it produces electricity by rotation

subject: science
stem:
For a school science exhibition, Meena's teacher asks her to choose a cell for a portable torch that students will carry around the classroom. Meena reads that a dry cell keeps its electrolyte as a moist paste rather than a free-flowing liquid, while a Voltaic cell contains a liquid electrolyte.
Which statement about the dry cell is correct?

options.A: It contains a liquid electrolyte that can spill easily, so it is best for the portable torch.
options.B: Its electrolyte is held as a moist paste, so it can be carried and used conveniently in everyday devices.
options.C: It is called dry because it contains no electrolyte at all inside it.
options.D: It must always be kept in one fixed position, so it is less convenient than a Voltaic cell.

subject: science
stem:
Meena's father buys a new battery for the torch used at their home in Jaipur. The shopkeeper tells them that this battery can be connected to a charger again and again, so it can be used for many months instead of being thrown away after it is used up once.
Which statement correctly classifies this battery?

options.A: It is a single-use cell because all batteries stop working after some time.
options.B: It is a rechargeable cell because it can be recharged and reused many times.
options.C: It is a single-use cell because it is used inside a torch.
options.D: It is a rechargeable cell because it is sold in a shop and not made at home.

subject: science
stem:
Meera's father buys batteries for the torch used during power cuts at their home in Pune. He wants to know which battery can be recharged and reused many times instead of being thrown away after one use.
Which statement correctly classifies a battery as rechargeable?

options.A: A battery is rechargeable if it gives a large current the first time it is used.
options.B: A battery is rechargeable if it can be connected to a charger and used again for many cycles.
options.C: A battery is rechargeable if it is small and light enough to fit inside a torch.
options.D: A battery is rechargeable if it stops working completely after one use.

subject: science
stem:
Meena is helping her grandmother in the kitchen. She pushes a heavy steel cupboard to make space near the wall, and the cupboard slides across the floor.
Which statement correctly identifies a force and the two interacting objects?

options.A: Meena's push on the cupboard is a force; the interacting objects are Meena and the cupboard.
options.B: The cupboard sliding on the floor is a force; the interacting objects are the cupboard and the wall.
options.C: The heavy weight of the cupboard is not a force, so no objects are interacting.
options.D: Any movement is a force, so the floor alone applies a force to itself.

subject: science
stem:
Meena is helping her mother in the kitchen. She observes four different situations.

Which situation shows a force acting between two objects?

options.A: The warm steel spoon feels hot when Meena touches it.
options.B: Meena pulls the drawer handle and the drawer slides open.
options.C: The pressure cooker whistle makes a loud sound.
options.D: Sunlight falls on the kitchen window and brightens the room.

subject: science
stem: Vikram lists four playground events. Which row correctly names a force as a push or pull between two objects?

options.A: Row 1
options.B: Row 2
options.C: Row 3
options.D: Row 4

subject: science
stem:
Riya is helping her mother in the kitchen. She presses a ball of dough with her hands, and later she pushes a rolling pin that was lying still on the shelf, making it roll across the table.
Which statement about the effect of an applied force is correct?

options.A: A force only counts when it makes an object start moving from rest.
options.B: An applied force can change an object's shape as well as its state of motion.
options.C: A force changes the direction of an object first, and that change then produces the applied force.
options.D: An applied force can change the speed of an object but can never change its shape.

subject: science
stem:
Priya pushes a stationary shopping trolley in a supermarket, and it starts to roll forward.
What does this show about the effect of the applied force?

options.A: The force changed the trolley's state of motion from rest to movement.
options.B: The force only changed the colour of the trolley.
options.C: The force had no effect because the trolley was at rest.
options.D: The force changed the trolley's motion into a change of shape.

subject: science
stem:
Meera keeps her steel lunch box on the dining table and it stays at rest.
Which statement about the forces acting on the lunch box is correct?

options.A: No force acts on the lunch box because it is not moving.
options.B: The lunch box has balanced forces acting on it, so it stays at rest.
options.C: The lunch box will stay at rest only if all forces on it are removed.
options.D: An object at rest always has an unbalanced force acting on it.

subject: science
stem:
Meera places her school bag on a table. The bag does not move.
Which statement about the forces on the bag is correct?

options.A: No force acts on the bag because it is not moving.
options.B: Only gravity acts on the bag because it is at rest.
options.C: Gravity pulls the bag down and the table pushes it up, and these forces balance each other.
options.D: The table pushes the bag up harder than gravity pulls it down, keeping it still.

subject: science
stem:
Priya hangs a steel paper clip near a bar magnet on her study table in her classroom in Pune. The clip jumps and sticks to the magnet without the magnet touching it.
Why is the force between the magnet and the clip classified as a non-contact force?

options.A: Because the magnet touches the clip after it moves
options.B: Because the magnet acts on the clip without any physical contact
options.C: Because the clip is made of steel and steel is a metal
options.D: Because Priya is watching the clip move

subject: science
stem:
Meena hangs a steel paper clip from a thread and brings a bar magnet near it. The clip moves towards the magnet without the magnet touching it.
Later, she pushes her toy cart across the floor with her hand to make it move.
Which statement correctly classifies these two forces?

options.A: Both are contact forces, because in both cases something makes the object move.
options.B: Both are non-contact forces, because the paper clip and the cart both start moving.
options.C: The magnetic force is a contact force, while the muscular force on the cart is a non-contact force.
options.D: The magnetic force is a non-contact force, while the muscular force on the cart is a contact force.

subject: science
stem:
Rohan pushes his steel tiffin box across two different table surfaces at home.
On the smooth glass dining table the box slides a long way before stopping. On the rough wooden study table it stops much sooner.
Which statement correctly explains why the box stops sooner on the wooden table?

options.A: Friction acts only after the box has stopped, so it pulls the box backwards on the wooden table.
options.B: The rough wooden surface has more irregularities, so it produces greater friction that opposes the motion and slows the box faster.
options.C: Friction is the same on both surfaces, but the box is heavier on the wooden table so it stops sooner.
options.D: The smooth glass surface produces more friction because the box moves faster on it.

subject: science
stem:
Priya slides a steel tiffin box across two floors of her house. On the smooth marble floor it travels far before stopping; on the rough stone floor it stops much sooner.
Which row correctly describes the friction acting on the moving tiffin box and the reason the rough stone floor stops it sooner?

options.A: friction opposes the motion; the rough surface has more irregularities that grip the box and increase friction
options.B: friction helps the motion; the rough surface pushes the box forward more strongly
options.C: friction acts only after the box stops; the rough surface holds the box still once it has stopped
options.D: friction opposes the motion; friction is the same on both floors, so the box stops sooner only because of gravity

subject: science
stem:
Meera holds a bar magnet a few centimetres above some iron pins on her study table at home. The pins jump up and stick to the magnet, even though the magnet never touches them.
Which statement correctly describes the force acting on the pins?

options.A: The magnet pulls the pins only after touching them, so the force acts with contact.
options.B: The magnet exerts a magnetic force on the iron pins, and this force acts without contact.
options.C: The pins rise because air pushes them up, so no force from the magnet is involved.
options.D: The magnet can only attract objects that are already magnets, so the pins must be magnets first.

subject: science
stem:
Ravi holds a bar magnet above an iron nail lying on his study table.
Before the magnet touches the nail, the nail jumps up and sticks to the magnet.
Which statement correctly explains why the nail moves?

options.A: The magnet pushes the nail away because of magnetic force.
options.B: Magnetic force acts on the iron nail without any contact between the magnet and the nail.
options.C: The nail moves because of gravitational force between the magnet and the nail.
options.D: The magnet can only exert a force on the nail after touching it.

subject: science
stem:
Priya rubs a plastic comb on her dry hair and holds it near tiny pieces of paper on her study table. The paper pieces jump up and stick to the comb.
Her brother Aarav then rubs a second comb in the same way and brings the two charged combs near each other.
Which statement about these observations is correct?

options.A: The paper sticks because the comb acquires the same type of charge as the paper.
options.B: The two charged combs repel each other because they carry similar charges.
options.C: The two charged combs attract each other because they carry opposite charges.
options.D: The paper sticks to the comb because of the magnetic force of the comb.

subject: science
stem:
Priya rubs two balloons on her woollen shawl during winter in Jaipur. She then brings the two rubbed balloons close to each other.
What will the balloons do, and why?

options.A: They attract each other, because rubbing makes the balloons sticky.
options.B: They repel each other, because both balloons carry the same kind of charge.
options.C: They attract each other, because both balloons carry the same kind of charge.
options.D: Nothing happens, because the balloons are uncharged after rubbing.

subject: science
stem:
Meena throws a ball straight up into the air in her school playground. The ball slows down, stops for a moment, and then falls back to the ground, speeding up as it comes down.
Which statement correctly explains the motion of the ball?

options.A: The Earth pulls the ball towards itself with an attractive gravitational force, which slows the ball on the way up and speeds it up on the way down.
options.B: The ball carries an upward force from the throw until this force runs out, and the Earth pulls the ball only after it starts falling.
options.C: The Earth's gravitational force acts only when the ball is touching the ground, so the ball slows down on its own while going up.
options.D: The Earth pushes the ball upwards while it rises and pulls it downwards only at the highest point.

subject: science
stem:
Ravi drops a small rubber ball from the roof of his school building. As the ball falls towards the ground, air resistance acts on it, and this air resistance eventually becomes constant.
Which description of the successive stages of the ball's motion is correct?

options.A: constant acceleration, then constant deceleration
options.B: increasing acceleration, then constant acceleration
options.C: decreasing acceleration, then zero acceleration
options.D: decreasing acceleration, then constant deceleration

subject: science
stem:
Priya hangs a metal pot from a spring balance in her kitchen and notes the reading.
What does this reading measure, and in which unit should it be written?

options.A: the mass of the pot, in kilograms
options.B: the weight of the pot, the pull of the Earth on it, in newtons
options.C: the density of the pot, in grams per cubic centimetre
options.D: the volume of the pot, in litres

subject: science
stem:
Meena ties a 2 kg bag of rice to a spring balance in her kitchen in Kochi. She knows that the Earth pulls the bag downwards. Her brother says the reading should be written in kilograms, but Meena says weight is a force.
What is the weight of the bag, and in which unit should it be measured?

options.A: The weight is the Earth's pull on the bag and it is measured in newtons.
options.B: The weight is the Earth's pull on the bag and it is measured in kilograms.
options.C: The weight is the amount of matter in the bag and it is measured in newtons.
options.D: The weight is the amount of matter in the bag and it is measured in kilograms.

subject: science
stem:
Meera has a spring balance at home to weigh vegetables.
On its scale, the difference between two consecutive numbered marks is 2 N, and there are 10 equal small divisions between them.
What is the smallest value of weight she can read on this spring balance?

options.C: 2 N

subject: science
stem:
Meena uses a spring balance in her school laboratory to weigh a bag of rice. On the scale, the marks for 2 N and 3 N have 5 small divisions between them.

What is the smallest weight value that Meena can read on this spring balance?

subject: science
stem:
Priya carries her school bag from her home in Delhi to a science camp on the Moon. The bag contains the same books in both places.
Which row correctly describes the mass and the weight of the bag on the Moon compared with on the Earth?

options.A: mass decreases; weight decreases
options.B: mass stays the same; weight decreases
options.C: mass stays the same; weight stays the same
options.D: mass decreases; weight stays the same

subject: science
stem:
Priya carries her schoolbag from her home in Delhi to a camp on the Moon, where gravity is weaker.
Which statement about the bag is correct?

options.A: Its mass is smaller on the Moon because gravity is weaker there.
options.B: Its weight is smaller on the Moon, but its mass stays the same.
options.C: Its weight and its mass are both greater on the Moon.
options.D: Its mass and its weight both stay exactly the same on the Moon.

subject: science
stem:
Meera lowers a metal bucket into the well at her grandmother's house in Kerala. She notices that the bucket feels much lighter while it is under water than when she lifts it out into the air.

Which statement correctly explains why the immersed bucket feels lighter?

options.A: The water removes the force of gravity acting on the bucket, so there is no downward force on it.
options.B: The water applies an upward force on the bucket, equal to the weight of water it displaces, while gravity still pulls it down.
options.C: The bucket's mass decreases while it is immersed, so it weighs less under water.
options.D: The water pushes down on the top of the bucket harder than it pushes up from below.

subject: science
stem:
Meena lowers a metal bucket into a bucket of water in her kitchen.
She notices that the bucket feels much lighter inside the water than in the air, even though she is holding it the same way.
Why does the bucket feel lighter in the water?

options.A: The water removes the force of gravity acting on the bucket.
options.B: The water pushes the bucket upward with a force equal to the weight of water it displaces.
options.C: The mass of the bucket decreases when it enters the water.
options.D: The air inside the bucket makes it float like a balloon.

subject: science
stem:
Meena stands on soft mud in her school playground wearing flat sandals. She then changes into high-heeled shoes and stands on the same mud with the same body weight.
Which statement about the pressure she exerts on the mud is correct?

options.A: The pressure is greater in the high heels, because the same weight acts on a smaller contact area.
options.B: The pressure is smaller in the high heels, because the weight is spread over a smaller area.
options.C: The pressure stays the same, because her weight does not change.
options.D: The pressure is greater in the flat sandals, because a larger area always gives greater pressure.

subject: science
stem:
Priya is fixing a notice board at home. She presses a drawing pin into the board with her thumb. The pin has a broad flat head and a sharp pointed tip.

She pushes with a force of 20 N. The flat head has an area of 1 cm² and the pointed tip has an area of 0.01 cm².

Which statement about the pressure is correct?

options.A: Doubling the area of contact doubles the pressure for the same force.
options.B: The pressure on Priya's thumb and the pressure on the board are equal because the force is the same.
options.C: For the same perpendicular force, a smaller area of contact gives a greater pressure.
options.D: The sharp tip gives less pressure because it feels lighter on the board.

subject: science
stem:
Radha's house has an overhead water tank on the roof, and a tap is fixed near the floor of the bathroom on the ground floor. She wants to know what decides the pressure of the water at the tap.
On which of these does the water pressure at the tap depend?

options.A: the total amount of water stored in the tank
options.B: the width of the overhead tank
options.C: the height of the water surface in the tank above the tap
options.D: the material of which the tank is made

subject: science
stem:
Meena's school has two water tanks on the roof. Tank P is tall and narrow, and the water level in it is 4.0 m above the ground-floor tap. Tank Q is short and wide, holds much more water in total, but the water level in it is only 2.5 m above an identical ground-floor tap.
Both taps are opened fully. Which statement about the water pressure at the taps is correct?

options.A: The tap from tank P has greater pressure, because the height of water above it is greater.
options.B: The tap from tank Q has greater pressure, because tank Q holds more water in total.
options.C: Both taps have equal pressure, because both tanks are on the same roof.
options.D: The tap from tank Q has greater pressure, because a wider tank pushes water out faster.

subject: science
stem:
Meena fills a tall plastic bottle completely with water and closes the cap tightly.
She then makes a small hole in the side wall of the bottle, near the bottom.
What does Meena observe, and what does it show about the pressure exerted by water?

options.A: No water comes out, because water pushes only downward on the bottom of the bottle
options.B: Water flows out through the hole, showing that water also pushes on the side walls of the bottle
options.C: No water comes out, because the cap is closed and air cannot enter the bottle
options.D: Water flows out only if the bottle is squeezed, showing that water does not push on the side walls by itself

subject: science
stem:
Meera fills a tall plastic bottle with water and makes three small holes at different heights on the side of the bottle. Water spurts out from each hole.
What does this show about the pressure exerted by the water?

options.A: Water exerts pressure only downward on the bottom of the bottle.
options.B: Water exerts pressure on the side walls of the bottle, and this pressure increases with depth.
options.C: Water exerts pressure only when the bottle is shaken.
options.D: Water exerts equal pressure at every point in the bottle.

subject: science
stem:
Meena presses a rubber sucker hook onto a smooth steel almirah in her kitchen, and it stays firmly in place. Her brother says it sticks because rubber is naturally sticky. Meena says air pressure is responsible.
Which statement correctly explains why the sucker sticks?

options.A: The rubber surface is sticky, so it grips the steel; air pressure plays no role.
options.B: Pressing the sucker pushes air out, so the higher atmospheric pressure outside presses it against the steel.
options.C: Air pressure inside the sucker increases and pushes it onto the steel.
options.D: The steel almirah attracts the rubber sucker like a magnet attracts iron.

subject: science
stem:
Meena presses a rubber sucker hook onto a smooth glass window in her kitchen. After she pushes out the air from inside the sucker, it stays firmly attached to the glass.
Why does the sucker stick to the glass?

options.A: The rubber of the sucker is sticky and glues itself to the glass.
options.B: The atmospheric pressure outside the sucker is greater than the pressure inside it.
options.C: The glass pulls the sucker towards it with a magnetic force.
options.D: The weight of the sucker is too small for it to fall down.

subject: science
stem:
On a hot afternoon in Jaipur, Ravi opens a window of his classroom. The air pressure inside the room is higher than the air pressure outside, and the two regions are connected through the open window.
Which statement about the air flow is correct?

options.A: Air flows from outside into the room because air moves from lower pressure to higher pressure.
options.B: Air flows from the room to the outside, and it flows faster when the pressure difference is larger.
options.C: Air does not flow at all because the pressure difference keeps the air at rest.
options.D: Air flows from outside into the room, and a larger pressure difference makes the flow slower.

subject: science
stem:
Meena opens the window of her warm kitchen. The air pressure inside the kitchen is higher than the air pressure outside, and the window is open so air can move between the two regions.
What happens to the air?

options.A: Air flows from outside to inside, and the flow gets faster as the pressure difference gets smaller.
options.B: Air flows from inside to outside, and a larger pressure difference makes the air flow faster.
options.C: Air flows from outside to inside, and a larger pressure difference makes the air flow faster.
options.D: Air does not move, because air only moves when it is first pushed by a fan or wind.

subject: science
stem:
During a storm, strong wind blows fast over the tin roof of Meena's house in a village near Pune. The roof is lifted upward.
Which explanation is correct?

options.A: The fast-moving air above the roof has lower pressure, so the higher pressure of the still air inside the house pushes the roof upward.
options.B: The fast-moving air above the roof has higher pressure, and this higher pressure pushes the roof upward from outside.
options.C: The pressure of the fast-moving air above the roof is the same as the pressure inside, so the roof lifts only because of its own weight.
options.D: The pressure above the roof is lower simply because it is higher up, whether the air is moving or still.

subject: science
stem:
During a storm, strong wind blows fast over the sloping tin roof of Meena's house in Pune.
The air inside the house below the roof is still.
Why can the roof be lifted off?

options.A: The fast wind pushes the roof directly upwards from above.
options.B: The fast-moving air above the roof has lower pressure, so the higher air pressure below the roof pushes it up.
options.C: The still air inside the house has lower pressure than the fast-moving air above.
options.D: The wind increases the pressure equally on both sides of the roof, making it lighter.

subject: science
stem:
On a hot afternoon in her village in Rajasthan, Meena watches dark thunderstorm clouds build up over the heated fields. Her teacher asks her to explain how the heated land and the moist air above it produce a thunderstorm.
Which chain of events correctly explains the formation of the thunderstorm?

options.A: Rain clouds become heavy with water and simply fall down as rain.
options.B: Cool air sinks over the fields, creating high pressure that pushes the rain out of the clouds.
options.C: Moist air rises, cools and condenses into clouds, but no air flows in from surrounding areas.
options.D: The hot land warms the moist air above it; the warm air rises and creates a low-pressure region; cooler air flows in from surrounding high-pressure regions; the rising air cools and its water vapour condenses into clouds and rain.

subject: science
stem:
On a hot afternoon in a village in Rajasthan, Meena notices dark thunderclouds forming over the heated fields near her home.
Which sequence correctly explains how the thunderstorm develops?

options.A: Rain clouds become heavy and simply fall to the ground as rain.
options.B: The heated land warms the moist air above it, the warm air rises creating a low-pressure area, cooler air flows in, and the rising moist air cools and condenses into clouds and rain.
options.C: Cool air from the surroundings sinks over the fields, pushes the warm air down, and squeezes rain out of the clouds.
options.D: The sun heats the clouds directly until the water vapour in them turns into rain.

subject: science
stem:
During a monsoon storm over her village in Kerala, Meera watches lightning flash and then hears thunder a few moments later.
Her teacher asks her to describe what happens inside the storm cloud, in the correct order.
Which sequence is correct?

options.A: Thunder is produced first, and the sound of thunder then causes the cloud's charges to separate and form lightning.
options.B: Rubbing between water droplets and ice particles separates charges in the cloud, the charge buildup breaks down the insulating property of air, a sudden discharge produces lightning, and the rapid heating and expansion of air produces thunder.
options.C: Lightning occurs when two clouds physically collide, and thunder is the sound of the clouds crashing into each other.
options.D: The rapid heating of air produces thunder first, and the vibration of the air then pulls charges apart to create lightning.

subject: science
stem:
During a monsoon storm over her school in Nagpur, Meera sees a bright flash of lightning and soon hears thunder. Inside the storm cloud, strong winds make water droplets and ice particles rub against each other.
Which sequence correctly describes how lightning and thunder are produced?

options.A: Rubbing separates charges; charge separation builds an imbalance; the built-up charge breaks down the insulating property of air; a sudden discharge gives lightning; rapid heating and expansion of air gives thunder.
options.B: Thunder heats the cloud first; the heat separates the charges; the charges then cancel each other quietly; the cloud collapses to give the lightning flash.
options.C: Two clouds physically collide; the collision directly produces the lightning flash; the flash then separates the charges; thunder comes from the clouds breaking apart.
options.D: Air first becomes a perfect conductor; charges flow slowly and silently; the silent flow produces thunder; thunder then ignites the lightning flash.

subject: science
stem:
Meera reads in her school science book about a storm forming over the warm Bay of Bengal. Warm, moist air above the sea rises, and the water vapour in it condenses into raindrops, releasing heat. A low-pressure centre develops, called the eye.
Which row correctly describes how the cyclone forms and how the eye compares with the surrounding region?

options.A: forms over warm ocean water; eye is calm while surrounding regions have strong winds
options.B: forms over warm ocean water; eye has the strongest winds while surrounding regions are calm
options.C: forms equally over cold ocean water; eye is calm while surrounding regions have strong winds
options.D: forms equally over cold ocean water; eye has the strongest winds while surrounding regions are calm

subject: science
stem:
During a school geography lesson in Chennai, Meera reads that a cyclone developed over the warm waters of the Bay of Bengal. Her teacher asks the class how such a storm forms and what the region at its centre, called the eye, is like.
Which row of the table correctly describes the formation of the cyclone and the conditions in its eye compared with the surrounding region?

options.A: Warm moist air rises over the warm ocean and water vapour condenses; the eye is a calm, lowest-pressure region while surrounding areas have strong winds and heavy rain
options.B: Warm moist air rises over the warm ocean and water vapour condenses; the eye has the strongest winds and heaviest rain of the whole storm
options.C: Cyclones form just as readily over cold ocean water; the eye is a calm, lowest-pressure region while surrounding areas have strong winds and heavy rain
options.D: Cold dry air sinks over the warm ocean to start the storm; the eye is calm but at the highest pressure in the storm

subject: science
stem:
In a class in Kochi, Meera and Arjun list four activities. In which activities does the observation show that matter is made of extremely small particles and does not become nothing?

| activity | W | X | Y | Z |
| activity | grinding a piece of chalk into fine powder | burning a piece of paper to ash | water evaporating from a hot plate | dissolving a spoon of salt in water |
| observation | the powder still tastes and behaves like chalk | only ash and smoke remain | the water seems to disappear completely | the water tastes salty, so the salt is still present |

options.A: W and X
options.B: W and Z
options.C: X and Y
options.D: Y and Z

subject: science
stem: Priya grinds a piece of chalk into a fine powder and then stirs some sugar into a glass of water until it can no longer be seen. Which statement best explains what has happened to the chalk and the sugar?

options.A: The chalk and sugar have become nothing, because no large pieces can be seen.
options.B: The chalk and sugar are still present as extremely small particles that are too small to see.
options.C: The sugar has disappeared, but the chalk has changed into a new substance.
options.D: Grinding and dissolving destroy the particles of a substance completely.

subject: science
stem: Meera stirs a spoonful of sugar into a glass of water until no sugar grains can be seen, yet the water still tastes sweet. Which statement best explains what has happened to the sugar?

options.A: The sugar particles have disappeared, and only the sweetness is left in the water.
options.B: The sugar particles have separated and spread into the spaces between the water particles, so sugar is present throughout the water.
options.C: The sugar has melted into liquid sugar, which sits at the bottom of the glass.
options.D: Each sugar particle has gone inside a water particle, making the water particles sweet.

subject: science
stem:
Meena adds two spoons of sugar to a glass of water and stirs. After some time, no sugar grains can be seen, yet the whole glass of water tastes sweet.

Which statement best explains this?

options.A: The sugar particles spread out and occupy the spaces between the water particles, so sugar is present throughout the water.
options.B: The sugar particles melt into a liquid and float on top of the water, making it sweet.
options.C: The sugar disappears completely, and only its sweetness stays behind in the water.
options.D: Each water particle absorbs a sugar particle inside itself, which makes the water particle sweet.

subject: science
stem:
Meera keeps a steel tiffin box on her study table. She notices that the tiffin box always keeps the same shape and the same size, no matter where she places it.

Why does a solid like the steel tiffin box have a definite shape and a definite volume?

options.A: Its particles are tightly packed and attract each other very strongly, so they stay in fixed positions and only vibrate.
options.B: Its particles are tightly packed, and this tight packing alone holds the shape even though the particles attract each other only weakly.
options.C: Its particles move freely throughout the box but the hard outer surface stops the box from changing shape.
options.D: The fixed shape and volume of the box push its particles close together and make their attractions strong.

subject: science
stem:
Meera presses a steel tiffin box and a ball of wet sand in her kitchen. The steel box keeps its shape and size because its particles are ……1…… and the forces of attraction between them are ……2…… .

Which words correctly complete gaps 1 and 2?

options.A: 1 tightly packed; 2 very weak
options.B: 1 tightly packed; 2 very strong
options.C: 1 far apart; 2 very strong
options.D: 1 far apart; 2 very weak

tables: {"headers":["","1","2"],"rows":[["A","tightly packed","very weak"],["B","tightly packed","very strong"],["C","far apart","very strong"],["D","far apart","very weak"]],"row_labels":["A","B","C","D"],"caption":"","is_option_table":true}

subject: science
stem:
Meera's mother places a piece of solid ghee in a pan and heats it gently. The ghee becomes a liquid.

Which statement best explains why the ghee melts, and how its melting point is identified?

options.A: Heating makes the particles vibrate more strongly until they can leave their fixed positions; the melting point is the lowest temperature, at atmospheric pressure, at which the solid ghee becomes a liquid.
options.B: Heating makes the particles stop vibrating so they can flow; the melting point is the temperature at which the liquid ghee begins to boil.
options.C: Heating creates new particles that fill the gaps; the melting point is any temperature listed for ghee in a table of data.
options.D: Heating makes the particles larger so they push apart; the melting point is the highest temperature the solid ghee can reach before burning.

subject: science
stem: Meera's mother keeps a block of jaggery near the hot stove, and after some time it starts turning soft and syrupy at its melting point. Which statement best explains why heating a solid like jaggery or ice can make it melt, and why the melting point is used to identify this change?

options.A: Heating pushes the particles closer together until they stop moving, and the melting point is the temperature at which particles stop vibrating.
options.B: Heating makes the particles vibrate more vigorously until they can leave their fixed positions, so the solid becomes liquid; the melting point is the specific temperature (at atmospheric pressure) at which this change begins, so it can be used to identify it.
options.C: Heating turns the solid particles into gas particles straight away, and the melting point is the temperature at which the solid evaporates.
options.D: Heating changes the particles into a different substance, and the melting point is just a number chosen from a table for each material.

subject: science
stem: Meena pours 200 mL of water from a bottle into a round bowl in her kitchen. The water spreads to take the shape of the bowl, but its volume stays 200 mL. Which statement correctly explains this?

options.A: The water particles break down into smaller particles when poured.
options.B: The water particles can move and change positions while attractions keep them close together.
options.C: The water particles are tightly fixed in one position and cannot move at all.
options.D: The water particles are far apart and move freely in all directions like a gas.

subject: science
stem:
Meena pours 200 cm³ of milk from a bottle into a tall glass. The milk takes the shape of the glass, but its volume stays 200 cm³.

Which statement explains this?

options.A: The particles in the milk are fixed in one position and cannot move at all.
options.B: The particles in the milk can move and change positions while staying close together because of the attraction between them.
options.C: The particles in the milk move freely in all directions and fill the whole glass.
options.D: The particles in the milk are far apart, so the milk can be squeezed into a smaller volume.

subject: science
stem: Meena opens the lid of a pressure cooker in her kitchen in Jaipur, and the steam quickly spreads throughout the room. Which statement correctly explains why a gas, like this steam, does not have a fixed shape or a fixed volume?

options.A: Gas particles have a fixed shape but move slowly, so the gas takes the shape of its container.
options.B: Gas particles move freely in all directions and the forces of attraction between them are negligible, so the gas spreads to fill all the available space.
options.C: Gas particles are tightly packed together, so the gas expands when the lid is opened.
options.D: Gas is mostly empty space, so steam spreads by itself without the particles needing to move.

subject: science
stem:
Meera sprays perfume in one corner of her classroom in Jaipur. Within a few minutes, Ravi, sitting at the far end, can smell it.

Four students explain why the perfume gas has no fixed shape or fixed volume.

| student | P | Q | R | S |
| explanation | gas particles attract each other strongly and stay in fixed positions | gas particles move freely in all directions with negligible attraction between them | gas particles are far apart but move only in one fixed direction | gas particles move freely and spread out to fill all the available space |

options.A: P and Q
options.B: Q and S
options.C: R and S
options.D: P and R

subject: science
stem:
In Meera's kitchen there are four substances.

1. cooking oil in a bottle
2. salt in a jar
3. water in a glass
4. sugar grains in a tin

Meera says that anything she can pour out is a fluid. Her teacher explains that a fluid flows and does not keep a fixed shape, while a solid keeps its own shape even when poured.

Which pair of substances should both be classified as fluids?

options.A: 1 and 3
options.B: 1 and 2
options.C: 2 and 4
options.D: 3 and 4

subject: science
stem: Meera's science teacher asks the class to sort everyday materials into fluids and solids. Which set of materials should Meera classify as fluids because they flow and do not keep a fixed shape?

options.A: water and mustard oil
options.B: sand and rice grains
options.C: ice cubes and wax
options.D: chalk pieces and pebbles

subject: science
stem:
Ravi presses the plunger of a closed syringe filled with air and finds that the air can be compressed.

Air can be compressed because there are ……1…… spaces between its particles.

Pushing the plunger forces the air particles ……2…… together.

Which words correctly complete gaps 1 and 2?

options.A: 1 no; 2 closer
options.B: 1 large; 2 closer
options.C: 1 large; 2 further
options.D: 1 no; 2 further

tables: {"headers":["","1","2"],"rows":[["A","no","closer"],["B","large","closer"],["C","large","further"],["D","no","further"]],"row_labels":["A","B","C","D"],"caption":"","is_option_table":true}

subject: science
stem:
Priya fills a plastic syringe with air and closes its opening tightly with her finger. When she pushes the plunger in, the air inside is compressed into a smaller volume.

Why can the air in the closed syringe be compressed?

options.A: The air particles themselves shrink when the plunger is pushed.
options.B: The air particles are far apart with large spaces between them, so they can be forced closer together.
options.C: The air particles change into liquid particles when pushed together.
options.D: The air particles escape through the walls of the syringe.

subject: science
stem: Priya adds a spoonful of sugar to a glass of water and stirs. Her brother Rohan adds a spoonful of sand to another glass of water and stirs. Why do the sugar and the sand affect the water in their glasses differently?

options.A: Sugar particles fit into the spaces between water particles when they dissolve, but sand does not dissolve and its particles settle at the bottom.
options.B: Sugar particles disappear completely in water, but sand particles grow larger after stirring.
options.C: Sugar reacts with water to form a new substance, but sand evaporates when stirred.
options.D: Sugar and sand both dissolve fully, so both glasses behave in exactly the same way.

subject: science
stem:
Priya adds one spoon of sugar to a glass of water and stirs until it disappears. The water level drops slightly below the mark she had made on the glass.

Her brother Rohan adds one spoon of sand to another identical glass of water and stirs. The sand settles at the bottom and the water level rises above the mark.

Why do the sugar and the sand affect the water level differently?

options.A: Sugar particles fit into the spaces between water particles, but sand particles do not dissolve and take up space themselves.
options.B: All small solids behave in the same way when stirred into water, so the levels should be identical.
options.C: Sugar particles push the water particles apart, while sand particles fit into the spaces between water particles.
options.D: Sugar is heavier than sand, so it pulls the water level down, while sand floats and pushes the level up.

subject: science
stem:
Meera's teacher places a few grains of potassium permanganate into a beaker of water. The colour slowly spreads through the water without any stirring.

Which statement correctly explains why the colour spreads and how using hotter water would change this?

options.A: The colour spreads because water particles are in constant motion, and the colour spreads faster in hotter water because the particles move faster.
options.B: The colour spreads only because the beaker is shaken, and the temperature of the water makes no difference.
options.C: The colour spreads because water particles are still, and the colour spreads more slowly in hotter water.
options.D: The colour spreads because the grains push the water aside, and hotter water stops the colour from spreading.

subject: science
stem: Meena adds a few drops of red food colouring to two identical glasses of water, one with cold water and one with hot water, without stirring either glass. Which statement about what she observes is correct?

options.A: The colour spreads only after Meena stirs the water with a spoon.
options.B: The colour spreads faster in the hot water because water particles move faster at higher temperature.
options.C: The colour spreads at the same rate in both glasses because water particles do not move.
options.D: The colour spreads faster in the cold water because cold water particles move faster.

subject: science
stem:
At home in Pune, Aarav makes jaljeera by stirring mint paste, roasted cumin powder, salt, lemon juice and chilled water in a steel jug. The drink looks cloudy, and he can still taste the lemon and mint separately. No gas bubbles or new solid appear.

Which check best decides whether the jaljeera is a mixture?

options.A: It is a mixture only if the liquid becomes one even colour throughout.
options.B: It is a mixture only if the substances react and form a new substance.
options.C: It is a mixture because two or more substances are physically mixed and each keeps its own properties.
options.D: It is not a mixture because the separate tastes can still be noticed.

subject: science
stem: Priya's mother makes a glass of nimbu pani (lemon water) by stirring lemon juice, sugar and salt into water until everything dissolves. Priya looks at the glass and cannot see the sugar, salt or lemon juice separately. How should Priya classify this mixture, and why?

options.A: Uniform mixture, because the components are spread evenly throughout and cannot be seen separately
options.B: Non-uniform mixture, because it contains more than one substance mixed together
options.C: Uniform mixture, because the lemon juice gives it one colour that can be seen
options.D: Non-uniform mixture, because the sugar is heavier than water and settles down

subject: science
stem: Meera is helping her mother in the kitchen. She prepares four mixtures. In which mixture are the components spread so evenly that they cannot be seen separately, even with a microscope?

options.A: Salt dissolved completely in a glass of water.
options.B: Vegetable pulao with rice, peas and carrot pieces.
options.C: Mustard oil poured into a bowl of water.
options.D: Sand stirred into a bucket of water.

subject: science
stem:
Meena's teacher writes 'air' on the blackboard and asks the class how it should be classified. Meena knows that air contains nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour, and that these gases are mixed together without chemically combining with one another.

How should air be classified?

options.A: A compound, because it contains more than one kind of substance
options.B: An element, because the gases in it keep their own properties
options.C: A mixture, because several gases are present together without being chemically combined
options.D: A pure substance, because it looks uniform and has no visible parts

subject: science
stem:
During a science class, Meera opens the window and tells her friend Arjun that the air in their classroom is a mixture, not a pure substance.

Which statement best explains why air is a mixture?

options.A: Air is a mixture because it is invisible and looks the same everywhere in the room.
options.B: Air is a mixture because it contains several gases such as nitrogen, oxygen, argon and carbon dioxide that are physically mixed but not chemically combined into one substance.
options.C: Air is a mixture because two or more gases present together must react chemically and form a compound.
options.D: Air is not a mixture because the gases in it cannot be separated from one another.

subject: science
stem:
Priya's teacher keeps a bottle of clear lime water on the laboratory shelf. After a few days exposed to air, the lime water turns milky.

Which gas in the air reacts with the lime water to make it turn milky?

options.A: oxygen
options.B: nitrogen
options.C: carbon dioxide
options.D: water vapour

options.D: 1 oxygen; 2 calcium hydroxide
