subject: science
stem: Meera buys a packet of table salt from a shop in Jaipur. The label on the packet says '100% pure salt'. Her science teacher explains that in science the word 'pure' has a special meaning. Which statement about the salt in the packet is correct?

options.B: The salt is a pure substance in science only if it contains just one kind of substance with nothing else mixed in it.
options.C: The salt cannot be a pure substance in science because it is sold in a shop.

subject: science

options.A: A pure substance, because the label says it is 100% pure
options.B: A mixture, because it contains more than one kind of substance
options.C: An element, because it contains only one kind of atom
options.D: A compound, because all mixtures are compounds

subject: science
stem: Meena is helping her science teacher sort substances found at home in Delhi. Which statement about elements is not correct?

options.A: A pure substance made of only one kind of particle is an element.
options.B: The oxygen gas in a cylinder is an element, even though its atoms are joined in pairs as molecules.
options.C: When atoms join together to form a molecule, the substance must be a compound.
options.D: A copper wire contains only copper particles, so copper is an element.

subject: science
stem:
Meera collects four pure substances in her school science lab in Jaipur. She checks what kind of particles each substance is made of.

Which substance should she classify as an element?

options.A: distilled water, made of identical molecules each containing hydrogen and oxygen atoms
options.B: oxygen gas from a cylinder, made of identical molecules each containing only oxygen atoms
options.C: salt solution prepared by dissolving salt in water
options.D: sugar crystals, made of molecules containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms

subject: science
stem: In her school laboratory in Pune, Meena passes an electric current through water containing a little dilute sulphuric acid. She collects two gases in separate test tubes. options.A: Water is a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen gases that can be separated by filtering.
options.B: Water is an element because it produces gases when electricity passes through it.
options.C: Water is a compound made of hydrogen and oxygen chemically joined together.
options.D: Water is a pure substance that contains only oxygen atoms.

subject: science
stem: Meera heats some dry sugar in a dry boiling tube in her school laboratory. A black solid is left behind and droplets of water collect on the cooler parts of the tube. Which statement does not correctly use these observations to conclude that sugar is a compound?

options.A: The black solid is carbon, so sugar must contain the element carbon.
options.B: The water formed contains hydrogen and oxygen, so these elements must have come from the sugar.
options.C: The water droplets must have come from the air, so they tell us nothing about the elements in sugar.
options.D: Sugar breaks down on heating into simpler substances, which shows it is made of more than one element.

subject: science
stem:
Meera heats some sugar in a dry test tube in her school laboratory. She observes that a black solid is left behind and droplets of water collect on the cooler parts of the tube.

What does this experiment show about sugar?

options.A: Sugar is an element because it leaves behind only one black solid.
options.B: Sugar is a compound because it breaks down on heating to give carbon and water, showing it contains more than one element.
options.C: Sugar is a mixture because it gives two different products on heating.
options.D: Sugar is an element because the water droplets come from the sugar, not from the air.

subject: science
stem:
For a school science project, Meena mixes iron filings with sulfur powder in a dish. Her brother Arjun heats a similar mixture strongly in a test tube to form iron sulfide.

Which statement correctly compares the iron and sulfur mixture with the iron sulfide formed after heating?

options.A: Both the mixture and the iron sulfide can be separated using a magnet, because both still contain iron.
options.B: The mixture shows yellow and grey particles and its iron is attracted by a magnet, while iron sulfide is a uniform black substance not attracted by a magnet.
options.C: The mixture and the iron sulfide react with dilute hydrochloric acid in exactly the same way, giving the same gas.
options.D: After heating, the black iron sulfide is still a mixture of iron and sulfur, so it keeps their original properties.

subject: science
stem:
For a school science activity, Priya mixes iron filings with powdered sulfur in a china dish at home. Her brother heats a similar sample strongly and obtains a black solid, iron sulfide.

Which observation shows that the unheated sample is a mixture and not the compound iron sulfide?

options.A: A magnet pulls the iron filings out of the unheated sample, but the heated black solid is not attracted to a magnet.
options.B: The unheated sample has one uniform colour throughout, just like the heated black solid.
options.C: Both the unheated sample and the heated black solid give the same gas with dilute hydrochloric acid.
options.D: The heated black solid can be separated back into iron and sulfur using a magnet.

options.A: Because two substances are present together in the glass
options.B: Because the sugar was stirred into the water with a spoon
options.C: Because sugar and water are both pure substances
options.D: Because the sugar is evenly distributed throughout the water

options.D: water, because it is present in the largest amount

options.A: The undissolved baking soda dissolves, and more baking soda can dissolve at the higher temperature.

options.B: Place the spoon on the balance straight away and read the number shown, and read the water level at the top of the meniscus.

stem: In her school laboratory, Meena measures the density of mustard oil as 0.91 g/cm³. The density of water at the same temperature is 1.0 g/cm³. She divides the two values to find the relative density of the oil. Which statement about the relative density is correct?

options.A: It is 0.91, with no unit, because it compares the oil's density with the density of water.
options.B: It is 0.91 g/cm³, because relative density is just another way of writing density.
options.C: It is 1.1, with no unit, because water's density must be divided by the oil's density.
options.D: It is 0.91 g, because the unit of volume cancels out when the densities are divided.

stem: Meera measures the density of a copper vessel at home and finds it to be 8.9 g/cm³. The density of water is 1.0 g/cm³. She writes in her notebook: “The relative density of copper is 8.9 g/cm³.” Which statement about her answer is correct?

options.A: It is correct, because relative density has the same unit as density.
options.B: It is wrong, because relative density has no unit; she should write 8.9.
options.C: It is wrong, because relative density should be written in kg/m³.
options.D: It is correct, because copper is denser than water.

subject: science
stem:
Meena fills a balloon with air and ties its mouth tightly. She then places the balloon inside a freezer for some time.

The balloon shrinks slightly.

What happens to the density of the air inside the balloon?

options.A: It increases, because cooling brings the air particles closer together, reducing the volume.
options.B: It decreases, because cooling always decreases the density of a gas.
options.C: It stays the same, because the amount of air in the balloon does not change.
options.D: It becomes zero, because cooling stops the movement of air particles.

subject: science
stem:
Meera does a simple experiment at home. She fills a balloon with air and keeps a steel spoon in the kitchen. She then warms both gently in the sunlight and later presses the balloon with her hands.

Which statement about density is correct?

options.A: Heating the steel spoon spreads its particles apart, so its density decreases noticeably.
options.B: Pressing the balloon brings the air particles closer, so the density of the air inside increases.
options.C: Heating the air in the balloon increases its density because the particles move faster.
options.D: The spoon and the air change density equally because density never depends on the state of matter.

subject: science
stem:
Meena drops a small steel nail and a large wooden log into a tub of water at home.

The tiny nail sinks but the heavy log floats.

What is the correct explanation?

options.A: The nail sinks because small objects are always heavier than large objects.
options.B: Steel has a greater density than water, so the nail sinks, while wood has a lower density than water, so the log floats.
options.C: The log floats because bigger objects always float, whatever material they are made of.
options.D: The nail sinks because its surface is smooth, and smooth objects always sink.

subject: science
stem:
In her kitchen, Priya drops a steel spoon and a plastic spoon of the same size into a bowl of water. The steel spoon sinks because its density is ……1…… that of water. The plastic spoon floats because its density is ……2…… that of water.

Which words correctly complete gaps 1 and 2?

options.A: 1 greater than; 2 greater than
options.B: 1 greater than; 2 less than
options.C: 1 less than; 2 greater than
options.D: 1 less than; 2 less than

subject: science
stem: Meera notices that the shiny steel bowl used in her kitchen reflects her face from the surface that bulges outwards. Her brother Arjun says the spoon's hollow side also acts as a mirror. Which statements correctly describe these spherical mirrors?

options.A: The bowl's outward-bulging reflecting surface is concave, and the spoon's hollow reflecting surface is convex.
options.B: The bowl's outward-bulging reflecting surface is convex, and the spoon's hollow reflecting surface is concave.
options.C: Both the bowl's bulging surface and the spoon's hollow surface are concave mirrors.
options.D: Both the bowl's bulging surface and the spoon's hollow surface are convex mirrors.

subject: science
stem:
Meera's mother uses a shiny steel ladle in the kitchen. Meera looks at the inside of the ladle's bowl, where her face appears magnified and upright when she holds it close. The inside of the bowl is the reflecting surface, and it curves inwards like the inside of a spoon.
Which type of spherical mirror does this reflecting surface behave like?

options.A: a convex mirror, because the surface bulges outwards towards her face
options.B: a concave mirror, because the reflecting surface curves inwards
options.C: a plane mirror, because the steel surface is smooth and shiny
options.D: a convex mirror, because all shiny metal objects behave as convex mirrors

subject: science
stem:
Priya looks into three mirrors at a science exhibition in her school in Pune.
In mirror 1, her image is erect and the same size as her face.
In mirror 2, when she stands close, her image is erect and enlarged.
In mirror 3, her image is always erect and smaller than her face, no matter where she stands.
Which row correctly names the three mirrors?

options.A: mirror 1: convex, mirror 2: plane, mirror 3: concave
options.B: mirror 1: plane, mirror 2: concave, mirror 3: convex
options.C: mirror 1: concave, mirror 2: convex, mirror 3: plane
options.D: mirror 1: plane, mirror 2: convex, mirror 3: concave

subject: science
stem:
Meena stands in front of three different mirrors at a science mela in her school. In mirror 1, her image is erect and the same size as her. In mirror 2, when she stands very close, her image is erect and enlarged. In mirror 3, her image is always erect and smaller than her.
Which row correctly names the three mirrors?

options.A: Mirror 1: concave, Mirror 2: plane, Mirror 3: convex
options.B: Mirror 1: plane, Mirror 2: concave, Mirror 3: convex
options.C: Mirror 1: plane, Mirror 2: convex, Mirror 3: concave
options.D: Mirror 1: convex, Mirror 2: concave, Mirror 3: plane

subject: science
stem:
Ritu's father fits a convex mirror as the side-view mirror on his scooter. A similar convex mirror is also fixed at a sharp turn near her school gate.
Which statement best explains why convex mirrors are chosen for these uses?

options.A: Convex mirrors show objects at their actual size, so distances are judged correctly.
options.B: Convex mirrors form erect, smaller images and give a wider field of view, so more of the surroundings can be seen.
options.C: Convex mirrors form magnified images, so small objects behind can be seen clearly.
options.D: Convex mirrors converge sunlight, so the image formed is brighter than in a plane mirror.

subject: science
stem: Meera's father has fitted a convex mirror at the gate of their apartment building in Pune so that the security guard can watch a wide stretch of the road. Why is a convex mirror used here instead of a plane mirror?

options.A: It forms an image larger than the object, so vehicles look bigger.
options.B: It forms a real, inverted image that can be seen clearly at night.
options.C: It gives an erect, smaller image and a wider field of view of the road.
options.D: It reflects sunlight better, so it needs no electricity.

subject: science
stem: Priya shines a torch at a plane mirror in her classroom. The light ray strikes the mirror so that it makes an angle of 30° with the mirror surface. What is the angle of reflection, measured from the normal?

subject: science
stem:
Priya is doing a science activity at home. She shines a torch beam onto a flat mirror fixed on her study table. The beam hits the mirror so that the ray makes an angle of 25° with the mirror surface.
Her teacher says the angle of incidence must be measured from the normal, not from the mirror surface.
What is the angle of incidence?

subject: science
stem:
Priya does a light experiment at home in Jaipur. She shines a torch beam onto a small mirror lying flat on a sheet of white cardboard and marks the reflected beam on the sheet.
Her brother bends the cardboard and says the reflected beam, the incident beam and the normal can now lie in different planes.
Which statement is correct?

options.A: The incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray must always lie in the same plane.
options.B: The incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray lie in the same plane only when the sheet is flat.
options.C: The incident ray and the reflected ray lie in the same plane, but the normal may lie in a different plane.
options.D: The three lines never lie in one plane because light travels in straight lines.

subject: science
stem: Meena shines a torch onto a plane mirror fixed on the wall of her classroom. She holds a white sheet of card so that the incident ray and the normal to the mirror both lie along the sheet. What must be true for the reflected ray to appear on the same sheet?

options.A: The reflected ray always lies in the same plane as the incident ray and the normal, so it will appear on the sheet
options.B: The reflected ray lies in a different plane from the incident ray, so it cannot appear on the sheet
options.C: The reflected ray lies in the same plane as the incident ray but not the normal, so it may not appear on the sheet
options.D: The reflected ray can lie in any plane, so bending the sheet makes no difference to where it appears

subject: science
stem:
Diya shines a torch at a plane mirror, as in the diagram. The dashed line is drawn at 90° to the mirror.

Which statement about the incident ray, that dashed line, and the reflected ray is correct?

options.A: The dashed line is just another name for the incident ray, so only two lines matter.
options.B: The incident ray, the dashed normal, and the reflected ray all lie in one plane.
options.C: The three lines need not share a plane; only the hatch marks along the mirror matter.
options.D: The same-plane rule is only for curved mirrors, not for a flat bathroom mirror.

subject: science
stem: Meera shines a torch so that several parallel light rays fall on three different mirrors in her science lab at school: a plane mirror, a concave mirror and a convex mirror. Which row correctly describes how the parallel rays are reflected by all three mirrors?

options.A: All three mirrors reflect the parallel rays as parallel rays, because each ray obeys the law of reflection.
options.B: The plane mirror keeps the rays parallel, the concave mirror makes them converge, and the convex mirror makes them diverge.
options.C: The plane mirror keeps the rays parallel, the concave mirror makes them diverge, and the convex mirror makes them converge.
options.D: The plane mirror makes the rays converge, the concave mirror keeps them parallel, and the convex mirror makes them diverge.

subject: science
stem:
Priya shines three narrow, parallel beams of light at a convex mirror fitted on the gate of her house.
How will the beams travel after reflection from the mirror?

options.A: They remain parallel to each other.
options.B: They converge to a point in front of the mirror.
options.C: They diverge as if coming from a point behind the mirror.
options.D: They are absorbed by the mirror surface.

subject: science
stem:
Imran sends several torch rays that are parallel to one another onto the same plane mirror shown below.

What happens to those rays after reflection?

options.A: They must meet at a point behind the mirror, because that is what every mirror does.
options.B: They stay parallel to one another after reflection from the flat sheet.
options.C: They spread apart as if the sheet were a convex surface, even though the sheet is flat.
options.D: Only the hatch marks on the back of the mirror decide whether the rays meet.

subject: science
stem:
Meera places a concave mirror facing the Sun outside her home in Jaipur. The reflected sunlight forms a small bright spot on a piece of paper, and the paper starts to smoke.
Why does the concave mirror make the paper hot enough to smoke?

options.A: The mirror absorbs the sunlight and becomes hot, and the paper touching the mirror's surface gets heated.
options.B: The mirror spreads the sunlight evenly over the paper, so the whole sheet slowly warms up.
options.C: The mirror is curved inward, so it converges the reflected sunlight into a small spot where concentrated energy raises the temperature.
options.D: The mirror reflects light without any focusing, but paper always catches fire when sunlight falls on it.

subject: science
stem:
Meera uses a concave shaving mirror to focus sunlight onto a dry scrap of newspaper in her courtyard. After a few moments, the paper begins to smoke at one small bright spot.
Why does the paper start to burn at that spot?

options.A: The mirror makes the sunlight warm as soon as the light touches the mirror's surface, and this heat passes to the paper.
options.B: The concave mirror reflects the parallel rays of sunlight so that they meet at one small point, concentrating the light energy there and raising the temperature enough to ignite the paper.
options.C: The mirror spreads the sunlight evenly over the paper, so the whole sheet warms up slowly until it catches fire.
options.D: The shiny surface of the mirror produces its own heat, which is transferred to the newspaper placed near it.

subject: science
stem:
Priya finds four transparent curved objects in her grandfather's old spectacle repair box at home in Jaipur. She wants to identify the convex lens by checking how its thickness changes from the middle to the edges.
Which object is the convex lens?

options.A: an object that is thicker at the edges than in the middle
options.B: an object that is thicker in the middle than at the edges
options.C: an object that has the same thickness all over
options.D: an object that is thick in the middle but does not let light pass through

subject: science
stem:
Meena finds four transparent curved objects in her grandfather's old spectacle kit at home in Jaipur. She measures how the thickness of each object changes from its middle to its edge.
Which object is a convex lens?

options.A: a glass piece that is thinner in the middle than at the edges
options.B: a glass piece that is thicker in the middle than at the edges
options.C: a glass piece that has the same thickness in the middle and at the edges
options.D: a glass piece that is curved but thicker on one side than the other

subject: science
stem:
Meera looks at a small flower through three different transparent objects from her science kit, holding each one close to the flower.

Through which one will the flower appear erect and enlarged?

options.A: a convex lens
options.B: a concave lens
options.C: a flat transparent glass window pane
options.D: a flat mirror

subject: science
stem:
Meena looks at a small printed word in her textbook by holding a convex lens close to the page. Later she holds a flat transparent glass pane over the same word.
How does the word appear through each material?

options.A: The word appears erect and enlarged through the convex lens, but the same size and shape through the flat glass pane.
options.B: The word appears erect and enlarged through both the convex lens and the flat glass pane.
options.C: The word appears smaller through the convex lens, but the same size and shape through the flat glass pane.
options.D: The word appears inverted through the flat glass pane, but erect and enlarged through the convex lens.

subject: science
stem:
In her school laboratory in Pune, Meera directs several parallel rays of sunlight towards four different transparent optical elements, one at a time.
Which element causes the parallel rays to come together and meet at one point after passing through it?

options.A: a thin glass plate with flat, parallel faces
options.B: a convex lens that is thicker in the middle
options.C: a concave lens that is thinner in the middle
options.D: a rectangular glass block placed at a small tilt

subject: science
stem:
Meera is doing a science project at home. She directs several parallel rays of sunlight towards three transparent objects one by one: a thin flat glass plate, a convex lens, and a concave lens.
She observes what happens to the rays after they pass through each object.
Which row correctly describes what happens to the parallel rays?

options.A: thin glass plate: converge convex lens: converge concave lens: diverge
options.B: thin glass plate: pass through unchanged convex lens: converge concave lens: diverge
options.C: thin glass plate: diverge convex lens: converge concave lens: pass through unchanged
options.D: thin glass plate: pass through unchanged convex lens: diverge concave lens: converge

subject: science
stem: Meena's father is setting up a shaving mirror at home that must give an enlarged image of the face, and her school is making a solar cooker that must concentrate sunlight at one point. Which optical element should be used for both purposes?

options.A: a plane mirror, because it always shows things clearly
options.B: a convex mirror, because it gives a wide view
options.C: a concave mirror, because it can form an enlarged image and also converge light to a focus
options.D: a convex lens, because it can form an enlarged image but cannot be used in a solar cooker

subject: science
stem:
Meena, a dentist in Jaipur, wants to see an enlarged image of a patient's tooth during an examination.
Which optical element should she use, and why?

options.A: A plane mirror, because it always gives an enlarged image
options.B: A concave mirror, because it gives an enlarged image when the tooth is held close to it
options.C: A convex mirror, because it gives an enlarged image of the tooth
options.D: A convex lens, because it spreads the light evenly over the tooth

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem:
Meera watches the Moon from her balcony in Jaipur for a month. She notices that the bright part of the Moon looks different on different nights, changing from a thin crescent to a full circle and back again.

Which statement correctly explains what she sees?

options.A: The Moon's own shape changes as it moves around the Earth
options.B: The bright part of the Moon seen from Earth changes as sunlight falls on different parts of the Moon
options.C: The Moon makes its own light, and this light becomes stronger and weaker
options.D: Clouds and shadows cover the Moon, so its shape looks different

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem: Meera watches the Moon from her balcony in Jaipur every night for a month. She notices that the bright part of the Moon slowly changes from a thin crescent to a full circle and back again. What is the correct explanation for these changing shapes?

options.A: The Moon changes its own shape during the month
options.B: We see different amounts of the sunlit half of the Moon from Earth
options.C: The Moon makes more of its own light on some nights
options.D: Clouds cover different parts of the Moon each night

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem:
Dev sketches the Moon on five nights and sees the bright part change shape.

What is changing?

options.A: The Moon itself is swelling and shrinking, because phase is another word for size.
options.B: The bright part we see from Earth changes, even though the Moon does not emit its own light.
options.C: Earth sees only the night side, so the bright part we see is the Moon's unlit half.
options.D: The rule holds even if we drop the fact that the Moon does not shine by itself.

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem: Meera observes the Moon from her terrace in Jaipur on a full Moon night. Which statement about the Moon's position and phase is not correct?

options.A: On a full Moon day, the Moon is nearly opposite the Sun, so its illuminated half faces the Earth.
options.B: When the Moon is between the Sun and the Earth, it appears as a new Moon.
options.C: The phase of the Moon depends only on how bright the Moon appears at night, not on its position relative to the Sun.
options.D: As the Moon–Sun separation changes, the illuminated portion visible from the Earth changes, producing different phases.

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem: On a festival evening, Meena sees the Moon high in the sky at midnight, and it appears as a complete bright circle. Where is the Moon relative to the Sun as seen from Earth?

options.A: The Moon is nearly opposite the Sun.
options.B: The Moon is in the same direction as the Sun.
options.C: The Moon is between the Earth and the Sun.
options.D: The Moon is exactly above the Earth's poles.

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem: Meera watches the Moon from her balcony in Jaipur at 8 p.m. on Monday and sees it low in the eastern sky. Her grandmother says that on Tuesday at 8 p.m. the Moon will look different. What should Meera predict?

options.A: The Moon will be in the same place at 8 p.m. because it always follows the Sun's daily schedule.
options.B: The Moon will be in a different part of the sky and will rise later than it did on Monday.
options.C: The Moon will rise exactly at sunset every day, so its position cannot change.
options.D: The Moon will not be visible at all on Tuesday because it disappears after one night.

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem:
Meera looks at the Moon from her balcony in Jaipur at 9 p.m. on Monday. She looks again at 9 p.m. on Tuesday.

What will she most likely observe?

options.A: The Moon will be in exactly the same position in the sky.
options.B: The Moon will appear in a different part of the sky.
options.C: The Moon will not be visible at all on Tuesday.
options.D: The Moon will rise at exactly the same time as the Sun sets.

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem: Meera fixes a straight stick upright in her school playground in Jaipur and marks the tip of its shadow every few minutes. She wants to measure the length of one day, which is nearly 24 hours. Which observation should she use?

options.A: The time between the stick casting its longest shadow on two successive days
options.B: The time between the shortest shadow of the stick on one day and the shortest shadow on the next day
options.C: The time from sunrise to sunset on a single day
options.D: The time between the stick first casting a shadow in the morning on two successive days

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem: Meena places a straight stick upright on her school playground in Jaipur and marks the tip of its shadow every half hour from morning to evening, for two days in a row. Her teacher says she can use her readings to measure the length of one day, which is nearly 24 hours. Which method should Meena use?

options.A: Measure the time between the stick's longest shadow on the first day and its longest shadow on the second day.
options.B: Measure the time between the Sun's highest position (shortest shadow) on the first day and the Sun's highest position on the second day.
options.C: Measure the time from sunrise to sunset on a single day and double it.
options.D: Count the total number of shadow marks she makes between morning and evening on one day.

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem:
Meera's grandmother in Jaipur explains how people long ago kept time by watching the sky. Meera lists three time units: a day, a lunar month, and a year.

Which row correctly matches each time unit to the sky cycle that defines it?

options.A: Day – Earth's revolution around the Sun; lunar month – Moon's phase cycle; year – Sun's apparent daily cycle
options.B: Day – Sun's apparent daily cycle across the sky; lunar month – Moon's complete phase cycle of about 29.5 days; year – Earth's revolution around the Sun of about 365.25 days
options.C: Day – Moon's phase cycle; lunar month – Sun's apparent daily cycle; year – Earth's revolution around the Sun
options.D: Day – Sun's apparent daily cycle; lunar month – Earth's revolution around the Sun; year – Moon's phase cycle

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem: Meera's grandmother in Jaipur explains how people long ago fixed their calendar by watching the sky. Which statement correctly matches each time unit to the sky cycle that defines it?

options.A: A day is set by the Moon's phases, a month by the Sun's daily movement, and a year by the stars.
options.B: A day is set by the Sun's apparent daily cycle, a lunar month by the Moon's full phase cycle, and a year by Earth's journey around the Sun.
options.C: A day, a month, and a year are only calendar words and are not linked to any sky cycle.
options.D: A day is set by Earth's journey around the Sun, a month by the Sun's daily cycle, and a year by the Moon's phases.

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem:
Priya's grandmother follows a purely lunar calendar in which each month begins with a new Moon. Priya notices that over the years the same lunar month falls in different seasons.

Why does a purely lunar calendar not keep the same months aligned with the same seasons?

options.A: The Moon's phases change more slowly each year
options.B: The seasons are caused by clouds and rainfall
options.C: Twelve lunar months are about 354 days, shorter than the 365-day seasonal year
options.D: The Moon's light is brighter in some seasons

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem: Meera's grandmother follows a purely lunar calendar in which each month begins with a new Moon, and 12 such lunar months make one lunar year of about 354 days. Meera notices that a festival fixed to a particular lunar month falls in winter one year but, after several years, falls in the rainy season. Why does a purely lunar calendar not keep the same months aligned with the same seasons year after year?

options.A: The Moon's phases change randomly, so no calendar based on them can ever repeat in a regular way.
options.B: Twelve lunar months total about 354 days, which is shorter than the roughly 365-day seasonal year, so the lunar year ends earlier and the months drift through the seasons.
options.C: The seasons themselves become a little shorter each year, so the lunar months can no longer keep pace with them.
options.D: The Moon takes exactly 30 days to complete its phases, which matches the seasonal year, so any mismatch must be due to counting errors.

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem: Meera's teacher asks why solar calendars add a leap day about every four years. Which statement is correct?

options.A: A leap day is added because the Moon takes exactly 28 days to orbit the Earth.
options.B: Earth takes nearly 365.25 days to revolve around the Sun, so the extra quarter-days add up to about one full day every four years, and the leap day keeps the calendar aligned with the seasons.
options.C: Calendars have 365 days by rule, and leap years are just arbitrary extra days chosen by governments.
options.D: A leap day is added to correct the time Earth takes to spin once on its axis.

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem: Meera's school in Pune follows a solar calendar with 365 days each year, but every fourth year an extra day (29 February) is added. Why is this leap day needed?

options.A: The Moon takes extra days to orbit the Earth, so the calendar must be corrected.
options.B: The Earth takes about 365¼ days to revolve around the Sun, so the extra quarter-days must be collected to keep the calendar aligned with the seasons.
options.C: The extra day is added only as a festival holiday and has no scientific reason.
options.D: The Sun moves faster in some years, so the calendar must be made longer.

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem: Asha's family celebrates a festival that follows a luni-solar calendar, which adds an extra month every few years. What will Asha notice about this festival's date on the school (Gregorian) calendar?

options.A: It falls on exactly the same Gregorian date every year.
options.B: It moves through all the seasons over several years.
options.C: It shifts on the Gregorian calendar but stays within the same season.
options.D: It is celebrated twice every year without any pattern.

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem: Meera notes that Diwali, which follows a luni-solar calendar, fell on a different Gregorian date this year compared to last year, while the solar harvest festival Makar Sankranti fell on almost the same date both years. Why does Makar Sankranti stay on nearly the same Gregorian date?

options.A: It is decided by the full Moon each year
options.B: It follows the solar cycle, which matches the Gregorian calendar closely
options.C: An extra month is added to the calendar every few years
options.D: All festivals fall on fixed Gregorian dates every year

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem: Meera's teacher asks the class about the calendar printed beside the Gregorian dates on the school notice board. Which statement correctly describes the Indian National Calendar?

options.A: It is an official solar calendar used by the Government of India along with the Gregorian calendar.
options.B: It is a lunar calendar in which each month begins at full moon.
options.C: It is used only for festivals and has no official use in India.
options.D: It is a 354-day calendar that ignores the position of the Sun.

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem:
Meera notices that the school calendar shows both Gregorian dates and dates from the Indian National Calendar used on official government documents.

How should the Indian National Calendar be classified?

options.A: an official solar calendar used along with the Gregorian calendar
options.B: a lunar calendar based only on the phases of the Moon
options.C: a private calendar used only for religious festivals
options.D: an international calendar that has replaced the Gregorian calendar

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem: While watching the night sky from her rooftop in Jaipur, Meera notices a small star-like point of light moving steadily across the sky. Her grandfather says it could be an artificial satellite. Which statement about artificial satellites is correct?

options.A: Artificial satellites are natural objects like the Moon, so they can never be seen from the ground.
options.B: A moving point of light must be a star, because artificial satellites cannot be seen from the ground.
options.C: Artificial satellites are human-made objects that orbit Earth, and under suitable viewing conditions they can appear as tiny moving specks of light.
options.D: Old satellites and rocket parts burn up completely, so they never become space debris.

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem: Meera and her father watch the night sky from their terrace in Jaipur. She notices a small point of light moving steadily across the sky, unlike the twinkling stars. Her father says it could be an artificial satellite. Which statement about artificial satellites is correct?

options.A: Artificial satellites, like the Moon, are natural objects that orbit the Earth.
options.B: Artificial satellites are made by humans, can be used for mapping and communication, and old satellites can become space debris.
options.C: Artificial satellites can never be seen from the ground because they are too far away.
options.D: Artificial satellites shine by making their own light, just like stars.

subject: science
stem: During a school activity, Meena's teacher shows the class four places near their school in Jaipur and asks: which of these places can be called a habitat because an organism lives there and the place provides both living and non-living conditions needed for life? () A. An empty steel tiffin box kept in a cupboard, where no organism lives; B. The bark of a neem tree where ants and small insects live, and which gives them shelter, moisture and air; C. A clean glass bottle of drinking water sealed in the classroom, where nothing lives; D. A dry wall of the classroom with no plants or animals on it

options.A: An empty steel tiffin box kept in a cupboard, where no organism lives
options.B: The bark of a neem tree where ants and small insects live, and which gives them shelter, moisture and air
options.C: A clean sealed bottle of drinking water in the classroom, where nothing lives
options.D: A dry classroom wall with no plants or animals on it

subject: science
stem: Meera notices small green algae growing on the damp wall behind her school's water tank in Kochi. She says, "This wall is a habitat for the algae." Which of the following best supports Meera's statement?

options.A: The wall is a habitat because it is a large natural place like a forest or a pond
options.B: The wall is a habitat because algae live there and the wall provides non-living conditions like moisture, air and light that support their life
options.C: The wall is not a habitat because only animals, not algae, can have habitats
options.D: The wall is not a habitat because it is a man-made structure and habitats must be natural

subject: science
stem:
Meena counts 15 rose plants growing together in her school garden in Jaipur on one Monday morning. Her teacher asks: is this group a population?
To decide, check both conditions:
• all the organisms counted are of the same kind
• they are counted in the same habitat at a given place and time
Which row shows the correct decision for Meena's count?
all organisms of the same kind / same habitat, place and time

subject: science
stem: Meena counts the neem trees growing in her school garden in Jaipur on one morning in March. Her friend says this count is a population. Which condition must be true for Meena's count to be a population?

options.A: The count includes every plant and animal living anywhere in Jaipur.
options.B: The count includes only neem trees, all counted in the same school garden at the same time.
options.C: The count includes neem, mango and peepal trees counted in different gardens on different days.
options.D: The count includes all the neem trees in India, estimated from a book.

subject: science
stem: Ravi observes a small pond near his school in Pune. He notes all the Rohu fish in the pond, the water plants, the insects, and also the water, sunlight and mud, and how they interact. Which term best describes everything Ravi has observed?

options.A: A population, because the Rohu fish are one kind of organism
options.B: An ecosystem, because both living organisms and non-living components are included
options.C: A community, because there is more than one kind of living organism
options.D: A habitat, because the pond is where the organisms live

subject: science
stem:
Meera keeps a small glass tank at home in Pune. Inside the tank are six guppy fish of one kind, some water plants, snails, sand, and water. A biologist notes down everything in the tank, including the living organisms and the non-living parts, along with how they interact.

What is the best description of everything inside the tank?

options.A: a population, because the guppies are one kind of organism living together
options.B: a community, because it contains several kinds of living organisms
options.C: an ecosystem, because it includes different living organisms interacting with non-living parts
options.D: a habitat, because the tank provides shelter for the fish

subject: science
stem: Meena observes her school garden in Jaipur and lists four interactions she sees there. Which of these is an example of a biotic–abiotic interaction?

options.A: Sunlight warming the dry soil near the garden wall
options.B: A neem tree's roots absorbing water from the soil
options.C: A butterfly collecting nectar from a marigold flower
options.D: Two sparrows fighting over a grain of rice

subject: science
stem: In a school garden in Jaipur, Meera observes that the roots of a neem sapling absorb water from the soil. Which type of habitat interaction is this?

options.A: biotic–biotic interaction, because both the neem and the water are needed for growth
options.B: biotic–abiotic interaction, because a living plant interacts with non-living water
options.C: abiotic–abiotic interaction, because water and soil are both non-living
options.D: no interaction, because the soil and water never meet the plant directly

subject: science
stem:
In her school garden, Meena observes a hibiscus plant, a butterfly feeding on its nectar, and a sparrow eating insects.
The hibiscus plant makes its own food by photosynthesis.
Which feeding role does the hibiscus plant have in this ecosystem?

options.A: consumer
options.B: producer
options.C: herbivore
options.D: carnivore

subject: science
stem: In a school garden in Jaipur, Meena observes a sparrow eating grains scattered on the ground and also catching small insects. The science teacher asks: how is the sparrow correctly classified according to how it obtains its food?

options.A: producer, because it lives in the garden where plants grow
options.B: omnivore, because it eats both plant material (grains) and animals (insects)
options.C: herbivore, because grains form the largest part of its diet
options.D: carnivore, because it catches and kills insects

subject: science
stem: Meena sees these organisms in the school garden: grass, grasshopper, frog, and snake. Which list shows a valid food chain, arranged in the order in which one organism is eaten by the next?

options.A: snake → frog → grasshopper → grass
options.B: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake
options.C: grass → frog → grasshopper → snake
options.D: grasshopper → grass → snake → frog

subject: science
stem: In a pond near her village in Kerala, Meena observes the following organisms: algae, small fish, a crane, and mosquito larvae. The algae are eaten by the mosquito larvae, the mosquito larvae are eaten by the small fish, and the small fish are eaten by the crane. Which sequence shows a valid food chain for this pond ecosystem?

options.A: crane → small fish → mosquito larvae → algae
options.B: algae → mosquito larvae → small fish → crane
options.C: algae → small fish → mosquito larvae → crane
options.D: mosquito larvae → algae → small fish → crane

subject: science
stem: In the pond near Meena's school, algae are eaten by small fish, the small fish are eaten by a kingfisher, and the kingfisher is hunted by a kite. Which organism is at the third trophic level in this food chain?

options.A: algae
options.B: small fish
options.C: kingfisher
options.D: kite

subject: science
stem: In a pond near Meena's school in Nagpur, a food chain is observed: algae → small insects → small fish → large fish → heron. Meena says the large fish must be at the first trophic level because it is bigger and stronger than the other organisms. Which statement correctly assigns the trophic levels in this food chain?

options.A: The heron is at the first trophic level because it is the largest and strongest animal.
options.B: Trophic level is decided by body size, so the large fish is at a higher level than the heron.
options.C: The algae are at the first trophic level, the insects at the second, the small fish at the third, and the heron at the highest level.
options.D: All organisms in the pond are at the same trophic level because they live in the same habitat.

subject: science
stem: In her school garden in Pune, Meera observes the feeding relationships shown in the figure below (arrows point from the organism that is eaten to the organism that eats it). Which of the following statements about this diagram is correct?

options.A: It is a food chain, because it shows grass being eaten by a grasshopper.
options.B: It is a food web, because the grasshopper is eaten by both the frog and the sparrow, so several feeding paths are interlinked.
options.C: It is a food chain, because every feeding diagram drawn with arrows is a single chain.
options.D: It is neither a food chain nor a food web, because it contains more than three organisms.

subject: science
stem:
Riya draws this feeding diagram for a school garden in her science notebook. In it, grass is eaten by both a grasshopper and a rabbit; the grasshopper is eaten by a frog and a sparrow; the frog is eaten by a snake; the rabbit is eaten by a fox; and the sparrow and the snake are both eaten by an eagle.

What should Riya call this diagram?

options.A: A food chain, because it starts with grass, which is a producer
options.B: A food web, because the organisms are connected through many interlinked feeding paths
options.C: A food chain, because the arrows show the flow of energy in one direction
options.D: A food web, because it contains more than three organisms

subject: science
stem:
Fatima copies the feeding diagram shown below from a Class 8 field booklet.

Is the diagram a food chain or a food web, and why?

options.A: A food chain, because any diagram with arrows between living things is called a food chain.
options.B: A food web, because more than one feeding path reaches the leopard.
options.C: A food chain, because grass is drawn at the bottom so there can be only one sequence.
options.D: Neither, because the labels are animal names rather than the word producer or consumer.

options.A: the first listed feature should be third

options.B: the first listed feature is not used in this item
options.C: both third and second at once
options.D: the first listed feature should be third

subject: science
stem: After Diwali, Meena's grandmother adds fallen leaves and vegetable peels to the compost pit behind their house in Nagpur. A few weeks later, most of this dead matter has broken down into dark soil-like material. Which organisms are mainly responsible for this breakdown?

options.A: earthworms only, which eat all the dead matter by themselves
options.B: decomposers such as fungi and bacteria, which feed on dead matter and waste
options.C: green plants, which absorb the dead matter through their roots
options.D: birds and insects, which carry the dead matter away to their nests

subject: science
stem: In Meera's school garden, fallen leaves and vegetable peels are collected in a corner. After a few weeks the heap shrinks and turns into dark, rich compost. Which organisms are mainly responsible for breaking down this dead matter and waste in nature?

options.A: Fungi and bacteria, which act as decomposers
options.B: Earthworms, which eat all the dead matter completely
options.C: Green plants, which absorb the waste through their roots
options.D: Birds and insects, which scatter the waste around

subject: science
stem:
Meera's school in Pune has a garden pond with pondweed, small fish that eat the pondweed, and dragonfly larvae that eat the small fish. Kingfishers visit the pond to catch the fish.

One year, most of the pondweed dies after polluted water enters the pond.

What is the most likely effect on the dragonfly larvae in the pond?

options.A: Their population will increase, because the pondweed will no longer compete with them for oxygen.
options.B: Their population will decrease, because the small fish they eat will have less food and fewer fish will survive.
options.C: Their population will stay the same, because the loss of pondweed affects only the pondweed itself.
options.D: Their population will stay the same, because they can breathe oxygen directly from the air above the pond.

subject: science
stem: In a school garden in Pune, students have a small pond with pondweed, tadpoles and small fish. One season, a gardener removes most of the pondweed from the pond. What is the most likely effect on this ecosystem over the next few weeks?

options.A: Only the pondweed is affected; the tadpoles and small fish remain unchanged
options.B: The tadpoles lose a food source and hiding place, so their numbers fall, and the small fish that eat tadpoles are then also affected
options.C: The small fish population increases because there is more open water
options.D: The tadpoles increase because there is no longer any competition for food

subject: science
stem: In a school garden in Jaipur, Meera plants many sunflower saplings close together. After some weeks, the plants stay small and none of them grows too tall or spreads too much. Her teacher says this competition helps keep the garden balanced. Why does competition help maintain balance in this garden?

options.A: The plants stop using water and sunlight completely, so nothing in the garden changes.
options.B: Competition for shared sunlight, water and space limits the growth of each plant, so no single plant uses up all the resources.
options.C: Competition makes each plant grow faster, so all the plants become very large together.
options.D: Competition removes all the weaker plants, so the garden soon has no plants left at all.

subject: science
stem:
In a school garden in Pune, Asha notices that the grass, rose bushes and a neem sapling all grow in the same flowerbed. None of them grows very tall, yet no plant dies out and the bed stays green all year.
Which statement best explains how competition keeps this small ecosystem balanced?

options.A: Competition makes all the plants share their food equally, so every plant grows at the same rate.
options.B: Competition for limited water, sunlight and space restricts how much each plant can grow, so no single plant takes over the bed.
options.C: Competition removes all weak plants immediately, leaving more resources for the strong ones.
options.D: Competition stops plants from using water and sunlight, so the resources are saved for the soil.

subject: science
stem:
Meera notices that small insects live inside the flowers of the pumpkin plant in her school garden. The insects get food and shelter from the flowers, while the flowers are not helped or harmed in any way.
The relationship between the insects and the flowers is an example of

options.A: mutualism.
options.B: commensalism.
options.C: parasitism.
options.D: predation.

subject: science
stem: In a village field in Punjab, Meena watches cattle egrets walking beside grazing buffaloes. The egrets eat insects that the buffaloes disturb, so the egrets get food easily, while the buffaloes are neither helped nor harmed. Which type of relationship is this?

options.A: mutualism, because both the egret and the buffalo benefit
options.B: commensalism, because the egret benefits and the buffalo is unaffected
options.C: parasitism, because the egret benefits and the buffalo is harmed
options.D: competition, because the egret and the buffalo share the same food

subject: science
stem:
Ravi's school is near a forest where elephants sometimes enter the village farms. Which row correctly explains why the elephants move into the farms?
forest cover and waterholes dry up in elephants enter farms because vegetation decrease in the dry season the forest they prefer eating crops

subject: science
stem: Meera lives in a village next to a forest in Maharashtra. After two years of poor rainfall, many trees were cut and the waterholes inside the forest dried up. Her family noticed wild animals such as nilgai and wild boar entering their farm and damaging the crops. Which statement best explains why the animals moved into the farm?

options.A: The animals preferred the taste of crops, so they chose the farm over the forest.
options.B: The loss of vegetation and drying of waterholes reduced food and water in the forest, so the animals searched for these resources near humans.
options.C: The animals were driven out by tourists visiting the village during the festival season.
options.D: The crops released a smell that confused the animals and made them lose their way in the forest.

subject: science
stem:
Priya's school in Pune wants to manage its garden in a way that supports ecosystem health. Her teacher lists four possible practices.
For the garden to support ecosystem health, the practice must reduce pollution, protect biodiversity, keep the soil healthy, and remain sustainable over many years.
Which practice best supports ecosystem health?

options.A: Spraying chemical pesticides every week so that no insects at all are found in the garden
options.B: Replacing all the plants with one fast-growing vegetable crop to get the biggest harvest
options.C: Using compost from kitchen waste, growing a variety of local plants, and watering with collected rainwater
options.D: Burning the dry leaves and waste in the garden corner to clear the space quickly

subject: science
stem:
Meena's school in Pune sets up a small fish pond on the campus. The students must manage the pond so that it supports ecosystem health, not just fish production.
Which practice would best support the health of this human-made ecosystem in the long term?

options.A: Adding extra chemical fertiliser to the pond every week so the fish grow as fast as possible
options.B: Growing water plants around the pond, limiting fish numbers, and using kitchen-waste compost in moderate amounts
options.C: Removing all the pond plants so that more sunlight reaches the water for the fish
options.D: Releasing a new fast-breeding foreign fish species to increase the fish yield quickly

subject: science
stem:
Meera's class visited a village near a forest in Kerala. Her teacher asked, "How do ecosystems like this forest benefit people?"
Which statement best explains how ecosystems benefit humans?

options.A: Ecosystems benefit humans only when people build farms or factories on the land.
options.B: Ecosystems benefit humans only by giving wood for making furniture.
options.C: Ecosystems benefit humans because living and non-living parts depend on each other and provide services such as fresh air, clean water and fertile soil.
options.D: Ecosystems do not benefit humans because natural processes happen without people.

subject: science
stem: Meena's school in Pune has a large banyan tree and a small pond in its garden. Her teacher asks: which statement best explains how this ecosystem benefits the people in the school?

options.A: It benefits people only because the school planted and maintains it for decoration.
options.B: Its living and non-living parts depend on each other, giving people fresh air, shade, and water that support life.
options.C: It benefits people only when the pond water is collected and sold for drinking.
options.D: It provides no benefit because humans do not eat anything growing in the garden.

subject: science
stem:
Meera's teacher asks the class why Earth is able to support living things, while the Moon cannot.

Which statement gives the correct reason?

options.A: Earth supports life only because it has water, so no other conditions matter
options.B: Earth supports life because air, water, soil, food and shelter are linked together in a thin surface layer where living things exist
options.C: Earth supports life only because it is the largest rocky planet
options.D: Earth supports life only because it shines brightly in the night sky

subject: science
stem: Meera's teacher asks the class: 'Earth supports life, while the Moon does not. What is the best explanation for this?' Which answer should Meera give?

options.A: Earth supports life only because it has water, so no other conditions matter.
options.B: Earth supports life because many linked conditions, such as air, water, soil, food and shelter, are present together near its surface.
options.C: Earth supports life only because it is the largest planet with a solid surface.
options.D: Earth supports life only because it receives sunlight from the Sun.

subject: science
stem: Meera's teacher asks her class whether a planet's temperature can be predicted from its distance from the Sun alone. Which statement is not correct?

options.A: A planet closer to the Sun generally receives more heat from the Sun.
options.B: A thick atmosphere rich in carbon dioxide can trap heat and raise a planet's temperature.
options.C: The planet closest to the Sun must always be the hottest planet.
options.D: Venus is hotter than Mercury even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.

subject: science
stem: During a science class in Pune, Meera tells her classmate Arjun that the temperature of a planet can be known just by checking how far it is from the Sun. Which statement correctly tests Meera's idea?

options.A: Meera is correct, because the planet closest to the Sun is always the hottest planet
options.B: Meera is not fully correct, because a thick atmosphere that traps heat can make a planet hotter than a planet closer to the Sun
options.C: Meera is not correct, because distance from the Sun has no effect at all on a planet's temperature
options.D: Meera is correct, because a planet's atmosphere cannot change its temperature

subject: science
stem: Meera learns in her school in Jaipur that Earth supports life, while planets much closer to or much farther from the Sun generally do not. Which statement best explains why Earth's position around the Sun allows life to exist?

options.A: Earth's distance from the Sun keeps temperatures in a range where water can stay liquid, making life possible.
options.B: Earth is called the Blue Planet, so any planet with that label becomes habitable.
options.C: Earth's nearness to other planets in space allows water to flow onto its surface.
options.D: Earth's orbital distance is produced by the presence of liquid water on its surface.

subject: science
stem: During a school science exhibition, Meera builds a model of the Solar System. Her teacher asks why Earth, unlike planets much closer to or much farther from the Sun, can support life. Which property of Earth's position around the Sun makes life possible?

options.A: Earth is the largest planet, so it can hold more water.
options.B: Earth is at a distance where the temperature allows water to exist as a liquid.
options.C: Earth is the fastest-moving planet, so its water never freezes.
options.D: Earth is blue in colour, so sunlight is absorbed better.

subject: science
stem: For a school Science exhibition, Asha builds a model showing what would happen if Earth were much larger. She explains that Earth can remain habitable partly because of its size. Which feature of Earth's size helps it support life?

options.A: Earth reflects sunlight because of its pale colour
options.B: Earth's moderate gravity can hold a suitable atmosphere without crushing living things
options.C: Earth is close enough to the Sun to stay warm
options.D: Earth spins quickly on its axis

subject: science
stem:
In her school science exhibition in Pune, Meera builds a model showing what would happen if Earth were much larger than it is, so its gravity became much stronger.

Why would this make it harder for Earth to support life?

options.A: A much larger planet would always be too far from the Sun to stay warm.
options.B: Much stronger gravity could crush living beings and change the atmosphere the planet can hold.
options.C: A much larger planet would have no water on its surface.
options.D: A much larger planet would spin too fast for day and night to occur.

subject: science
stem:
During a class discussion, Meera says that the atmosphere is just the air around the Earth and only gives living things something to breathe. Her teacher asks her to think about what else the atmosphere does for life.

Which property of Earth's atmosphere, besides providing oxygen for respiration, helps make life on Earth possible?

options.A: It provides oxygen that humans, animals, and plants use for respiration.
options.B: It reflects all sunlight back into space so the Earth never warms up.
options.C: It traps some heat through a mild greenhouse effect, keeping temperatures warm enough for water to remain liquid.
options.D: It adds mass to the Earth so that objects stay on the ground.

subject: science
stem: For a school science project, Meena and Arjun discuss why life on Earth can survive. Their teacher asks: besides simply being the air around us, what does the atmosphere do that helps support life? Which statement is not correct?

options.A: It contains oxygen, which humans, animals and plants use for respiration.
options.B: It traps some of the Sun's heat, keeping Earth warm enough for water to stay liquid.
options.C: It completely blocks all heat from escaping, so Earth never cools down at night.
options.D: Its gases help keep temperatures mild enough for living things to survive.

subject: science
stem:
During a school science exhibition in Jaipur, Meera explains why Earth can support life while Mars cannot.

Which property of Earth is most important in protecting life from harmful particles coming from space?

options.A: Earth's magnetic field deflects harmful cosmic rays and solar-wind particles.
options.B: Earth's atmosphere gives the sky a blue colour.
options.C: Earth's surface is mostly covered by oceans.
options.D: Earth rotates on its axis once every 24 hours.

subject: science
stem: Meera reads in her science book at home in Jaipur that Earth behaves like a giant magnet. She asks her teacher why this magnetic field is important for life on Earth. Which statement gives the correct reason?

options.A: The magnetic field makes compasses point north, which helps sailors and travellers find direction.
options.B: The magnetic field deflects many harmful cosmic rays and solar-wind particles, protecting the atmosphere and living things.
options.C: The magnetic field pulls rain clouds towards the land, giving farms enough water.
options.D: The magnetic field keeps the Moon in orbit so that tides remain regular.

subject: science
stem: Meera studies her school garden in Nagpur to find out why plants grow well in some corners but not others. Which statement about how water, sunlight, and moving air help sustain life on Earth is not correct?

options.A: Sunlight warms water, which evaporates, forms clouds, and returns as rain that refills ponds, lakes, and wells.
options.B: Plants use sunlight to make food, so nearly all living beings depend on it for energy.
options.C: Because most of the Earth has water, the same plants and animals can live in every place on Earth.
options.D: Moving air carries water vapour and rain-bearing clouds, so rainfall differs from place to place and decides which plants and animals can live in each region.

subject: science
stem: Meena waters the tulsi plant in her courtyard in Jaipur every morning. One hot afternoon, she asks her teacher why the rain that refills their village pond and helps crops grow does not fall equally everywhere in India. Her teacher draws a chain showing how sunlight, water and moving air work together on Earth. Which chain is correct?

options.A: Rain fills ponds first, and then the Sun heats the rainwater to form clouds that bring more rain.
options.B: Sunlight heats water in ponds, rivers and seas; water vapour rises and forms clouds; moving air carries the clouds; rain falls and refills water sources, helping plants and animals live in a place.
options.C: Moving air cools the land first, which creates sunlight, and sunlight then makes rain fall from clear skies.
options.D: Because most of Earth is covered with water, every place gets the same rainfall, so the same plants and animals can live everywhere.

subject: science
stem: Meera's class is discussing why Earth can support life. Her teacher says that rocks, soil, minerals, and the variety of landforms are not just a lifeless background. Which statement best explains how these support living things?

options.A: Rocks are non-living, so they cannot help living things survive.
options.B: Rocks only make the Earth look different from other planets.
options.C: Soil formed from broken-down rocks and the remains of plants and animals holds nutrients like nitrogen and potassium, and varied landforms create different habitats where living things can grow and survive.
options.D: Minerals in the Earth's crust are useful mainly for making buildings and roads.

subject: science
stem:
For a school project, Meena's class in Pune discusses why the Earth can support living things while the Moon cannot. Meena says that the rocks, soil and minerals of the Earth's crust are just a lifeless background and do not really help living things.

Which statement best explains why Meena is wrong?

options.A: Rocks and minerals are non-living, so they cannot help living things survive.
options.B: Soil formed from broken-down rocks and the remains of plants and animals contains nutrients such as nitrogen and potassium, which plants need to grow.
options.C: The Earth's crust is useful to life only because it provides metals for making tools and buildings.
options.D: Geodiversity matters only because it makes the landscape look varied and beautiful.

subject: science
stem: Meera's school in Pune keeps a small garden pond with fish, water plants, snails and stones at the bottom. The pond stays healthy for years without anyone cleaning it. Which statement best explains how the pond keeps its balance?

options.A: The fish alone keep the pond balanced because they eat all the waste.
options.B: Plants make food, animals eat plants or other animals, decomposers return nutrients to the water and soil, and the water, sunlight and stones support all of them together.
options.C: The pond stays balanced only because animals and plants are present in the same place.
options.D: The non-living parts like water and stones do not play any role in the balance.

subject: science
stem: Meena waters the tulsi plant on her balcony every morning. Her grandmother says the plant, the soil, the sunlight and the water all work together to keep this small system balanced. Which statement about how this balance is maintained is correct?

options.A: Only living things like the tulsi plant and insects are needed for balance; soil, sunlight and water do not play any part.
options.B: Balance is maintained because living things depend on one another and on non-living things: the plant uses sunlight and water, insects take nectar, and decomposers in the soil return nutrients.
options.C: Balance is maintained only when plants and insects live in the same place, whether or not nutrients are returned to the soil.
options.D: The balance would remain the same if all the water and sunlight were removed, because the tulsi plant is a living thing.

subject: science
stem: Meera notices that the marigold plants grown from seeds in her school garden look very similar to the parent plant, but a few of them have slightly different flower colours. Which statement best explains how reproduction produces both this similarity and this variation?

options.A: Reproduction passes inherited instructions from parent to offspring, giving resemblance, while small changes in these instructions create variation.
options.B: Reproduction only makes exact copies, so variation must come from a completely separate process.
options.C: Reproduction creates variation first, and this variation then produces the inherited instructions.
options.D: Reproduction keeps the species alive, so the instructions passed to offspring do not matter.

subject: science
stem: Meera notices that she looks like her parents, but her younger brother Aarav has a slightly different eye colour. Which statement correctly explains how reproduction produces both similarity and variation in a family?

options.A: Reproduction passes instructions from parents to children, and small changes in these instructions can cause variation.
options.B: Reproduction makes exact copies of the parents, so any variation must come from a completely separate process.
options.C: Reproduction only creates variation and plays no role in keeping children similar to their parents.
options.D: Variation appears only when the environment changes, and reproduction has nothing to do with it.

subject: science
stem:
Priya notices that a new money plant has grown from a stem cutting her grandmother placed in a bottle of water at home.

Which statement explains why this is an example of vegetative propagation rather than reproduction by seeds?

options.A: The new plant grew faster than a plant grown from a seed.
options.B: The new plant grew from a part of a single parent plant, not from a seed formed by two parents.
options.C: The new plant grew in water instead of in soil.
options.D: The new plant has shiny green leaves like the parent plant.

subject: science
stem:
Meera's grandmother plants a small piece of ginger with an eye into the soil of their garden in Nagpur. After some weeks, a new ginger plant grows from this piece.

Which statement best describes how the new ginger plant was produced?

options.A: By seeds formed after the mixing of instructions from two parent plants
options.B: By vegetative propagation, because a new plant grew from a part of one parent plant
options.C: By two parent plants exchanging pollen and producing fruit
options.D: By a seedling sprouting from a seed buried in the soil

subject: science
stem: Ananya's class is discussing how sexual reproduction in humans passes on genetic information without the amount doubling in every generation. Which statement is not correct?

options.A: Each gamete carries half of a parent's genetic material.
options.B: A male gamete and a female gamete join during fertilisation.
options.C: Each child receives a complete set of genetic material from each parent.
options.D: The new cell formed at fertilisation contains a mix of information from both parents.

subject: science
stem: In her science class in Jaipur, Meena learns that a human sperm cell and an egg cell each carry half the genetic material of a parent. Why does sexual reproduction not double the amount of genetic information in every new generation?

options.A: Each gamete carries half of a parent's genetic material, so joining two gametes restores the complete set of genetic instructions.
options.B: The parents give their complete genetic material to the offspring, so nothing is ever lost between generations.
options.C: Gametes from the two parents avoid mixing, so each offspring is an exact copy of only one parent.
options.D: Only one gamete takes part in fertilisation, so the genetic material stays the same.

subject: science
stem: Meena sees bees carrying pollen from flower to flower in her school garden in Jaipur. Her teacher asks: where is the male gamete of a flowering plant found?

options.A: Inside the ovule in the flower.
options.B: Inside the pollen grain in the anther.
options.C: Inside the petals of the flower.
options.D: Inside the nectar at the base of the flower.

subject: science
stem: Meena is helping her teacher prepare a chart on reproduction for the school science exhibition in Jaipur. For the chart, she must state where the male and female gametes are found in a flowering plant. Which statement should she write?

options.A: Male gametes are in the ovules and female gametes are in the pollen grains.
options.B: Male gametes are in the pollen grains inside the anther and female gametes are in the ovules inside the flower.
options.C: Both male and female gametes are in the petals of the flower.
options.D: Male gametes are in the roots and female gametes are in the leaves.

subject: science
stem: Meena's hen laid a fertilised egg, and her cow Lakshmi is also expecting a calf. Which statement correctly compares where the fertilised egg develops in birds like the hen and in most mammals like the cow?

options.A: In both the hen and the cow, the fertilised egg develops inside the female's body until the young one is born.
options.B: In the hen, the fertilised egg is laid and the embryo develops during hatching, while in the cow the embryo develops inside the mother's body, which supplies food and oxygen until birth.
options.C: In both the hen and the cow, the fertilised egg is laid outside the body and the embryo develops during hatching.
options.D: In the hen, the embryo develops inside the female's body until birth, while in the cow the fertilised egg is laid and hatches outside.

subject: science
stem:
During a school visit to a poultry farm, Meena learns that a hen lays her egg soon after fertilisation, while her neighbour's dog carries her pups until they are born.

Which statement correctly compares where the fertilised egg develops in birds and in most mammals?

options.A: In both birds and most mammals, the embryo develops inside the female's body until birth.
options.B: In birds the embryo develops in a laid egg outside the body, while in most mammals it develops inside the female's body.
options.C: In birds the embryo develops inside the female's body, while in most mammals it develops in a laid egg.
options.D: In both birds and most mammals, the embryo develops in a laid egg outside the body.

subject: science
stem:
Meera lives near a busy road in Jaipur. Her family burns waste plastic in the courtyard, and nearby trees are being cut to build shops. Her teacher says such human actions threaten life on Earth.

Which statement best explains how these actions create major threats to life?

options.A: Burning fuels and waste releases greenhouse gases that trap heat, while cutting trees destroys habitats and disturbs the balance of living and non-living systems.
options.B: Burning waste and cutting trees are separate small problems, so they cannot disturb the balance that supports life on Earth.
options.C: Only factories in big cities release greenhouse gases, so actions at home like burning waste do not threaten life.
options.D: The disturbed balance of Earth systems comes first, and this is what causes human activities like burning fuels and cutting trees.

subject: science
stem: Ravi's class in Pune is studying why Earth supports life. His teacher asks which human action directly adds greenhouse gases to the air and so disturbs the balance that keeps Earth suitable for living things. Which action should Ravi choose?

options.A: Burning coal and petrol in factories and vehicles
options.B: Planting trees along the school boundary
options.C: Using rainwater harvesting tanks at home
options.D: Separating wet and dry waste for composting

subject: science
stem: Meera's school in Pune wants to help protect life on Earth. Some students say that one big action, such as recycling plastic bottles, is enough on its own. Which statement about protecting life on Earth is correct?

options.A: Life is protected only when many connected actions are taken together, such as cutting pollution, saving energy and water, and protecting biodiversity, because Earth's systems affect one another.
options.B: Recycling plastic alone is enough to protect all of Earth's life-supporting systems.
options.C: Earth's atmosphere, water, land, and living things are separate, so an action in one system cannot affect the others.
options.D: Only governments can protect life on Earth, so individual and community actions make no difference.

subject: science
stem: Meera's class in Pune is planning how to protect the local environment so that life around their school can thrive. Arjun says, 'If we just recycle the plastic bottles in our school canteen, all of Earth's life-supporting systems will be safe.' Why is Arjun's single action not enough on its own?

options.A: Because recycling plastic actually increases pollution in the air.
options.B: Because the hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere and geosphere are connected, so protecting life needs many linked actions such as saving water and energy and protecting biodiversity.
options.C: Because protecting life is only the job of governments, not of students and families.
options.D: Because one school is too small to make any difference to the environment at all.
